papers.contribution: Develops a Coasean stakeholder theory defining stakeholders by shutdown power over value-creating transactions.

papers.title: Regional Variations and Productivity Puzzles in Health Care
papers.summary: Higher-utilization areas show no better patient health, once read as evidence that costs could be cut without harm. New evidence shows meaningful supply-side and demand-side roles, substantial provider productivity variation, and little knowledge of area-level productivity sources. Greater engagement with the productivity literature outside health care is suggested.
papers.contribution: Reviews how understanding of regional health care variation has evolved, emphasizing supply and demand factors and productivity differences.
papers.q: What have we learned about regional variation and productivity in US health care since the 2000s?
papers.ident: Descriptive: literature review of regional variation and productivity in health care

papers.title: Who Can Control Our Firms? National Security and Foreign Ownership Regulation
papers.q: Why do governments regulate foreign ownership of domestic firms on national security grounds, beyond standard policy tools?
papers.summary: Ownership allocates residual control over non-contractible decisions, and absent enforceable agreements the costs of conflict shape geopolitical bargaining. Foreign ownership can raise dependence, technology transfer or sabotage scope. US regulation emphasizes national security risks of foreign control, has tightened with geopolitical tensions, and is tighter in sectors with more defense demand and contractual frictions.
papers.ident: Theory: property-rights model of multinational ownership and geopolitical bargaining, with descriptive evidence on US regulation
papers.contribution: Shows that contractual frictions make multinational firm boundaries central to geoeconomic policy, with ownership regulation as a second-best tool.
papers.dataDetail: US foreign ownership regulation and sector exposure to defense demand

papers.title: Comparative Advantage and Economies of Scale under Uncertainty
papers.q: How do uncertainty and economies of scale affect regional specialization and the gains from trade?
papers.summary: Empirically, changes in sectoral productivity volatility affect US regional economies as predicted. Calibrated on US commuting zones, uncertainty shifts employment away from riskier sectors and locations and lowers US aggregate gains from trade by around 20 percent. Agglomeration forces and elastic labor supply mitigate losses for regions that lose from trade.
papers.ident: Spatial equilibrium model with uncertainty calibrated on US commuting zones; reduced-form tests using volatility changes
papers.contribution: Builds a spatial equilibrium model with sectoral scale economies, aggregate uncertainty and irreversible worker mobility, and extends hat-algebra to uncertainty.
papers.dataDetail: US commuting zone data and international trade data

papers.title: The Returns to Temporary Migration: Experimental Evidence from the H-2A Program
papers.summary: In one US season migrants earn over USD 16,000 and send 70% to origin households. Food security rises and poverty falls by 10 percentage points; families invest in homes, durables and debt reduction, not businesses. Household respondents' mental health worsens, and 85% of migrants migrate again the following season.
papers.contribution: Provides experimental evidence from randomized H-2A visas on earnings, remittances, living standards and household spillovers.
papers.q: What are the returns to temporary migration under the US H-2A agricultural visa program for Mexican workers and their households?
papers.ident: Randomized allocation of H-2A seasonal visas among Mexican agricultural workers
papers.dataDetail: Surveys of Mexican migrants and origin households

papers.title: A Network Approach to Geopolitics

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.q: How can geopolitics be modelled as a network of coordination and strategic influence among countries?
papers.summary: Countries trade off domestic interests against aligning with connected countries and exert costly bilateral influence. The covariance matrices of domestic interests and geopolitical actions identify latent cleavages and the network. Implemented on UN voting and democratic orientation, the network is low-dimensional, aligns with external measures of ties and recovers known cleavages.
papers.ident: Structural network model identified from covariance of domestic interests and geopolitical actions, estimated on UN voting
papers.contribution: Develops a tractable framework with closed-form equilibrium that recovers geopolitical networks and cleavages from covariance of interests and actions.
papers.dataDetail: United Nations voting and democratic orientation data

papers.title: HouseholdBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as Predictors of Household Economic Behavior

authors.inst: London School of Economics and Political Science

papers.q: How well can large language models predict household economic behavior and responses to changing conditions?
papers.summary: Most LLMs beat a no-change baseline, including on policy-response tasks, with the best model lowering numeric error by 12.2%. Gradient-boosted trees rank first on most tasks; leading proprietary LLMs approach them, open-weight models lag, and LLMs systematically over- and underpredict. Fine-tuning and aggregating 16 predictions let a 4 billion parameter model match proprietary models.
papers.ident: Benchmark: prediction tasks from US household surveys comparing LLMs, a no-change baseline and gradient boosted trees
papers.contribution: Introduces HouseholdBench, uniting 6 US household surveys and 32 prediction tasks to evaluate 13 LLMs against baselines.
papers.dataDetail: 6 US household surveys with 32 prediction tasks

papers.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
papers.q: How do firms choose among incentive contracts, and how accurately do managers predict their effects?
papers.summary: The best-performing contract raises agent output and firm revenue by over 20% over the status quo despite being ranked lower by managers, while the worst performs as predicted. Managers identify underperforming contracts but underestimate top ones. Differences come from labor supply responses, and predictability depends on contract complexity and managerial hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: Contract design matters for firm performance and managerial cognition shows systematic limits in shaping incentives.
papers.ident: Market-level randomization of agents to expenditure-equivalent incentive contracts, with elicited manager beliefs
papers.contribution: Combines a survey of managerial beliefs with a large-scale field experiment randomizing expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes across markets.
papers.dataDetail: Field experiment with firm's agents and survey of managers' beliefs

papers.title: Salinization and Development,
papers.q: How does climate-driven salinity intrusion affect agricultural production, labor and household spending in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta?
papers.summary: Salinity reduces rice yields but causes disproportionately larger declines in output and revenue, driven by less cultivated land and limited switching to salt-resistant crops. Own-farm employment falls with minimal transition to non-agriculture. Households shift spending toward healthcare and children's schooling beyond Engel curve predictions.
papers.contribution: Maps localized hydrological shocks using river salinity and canal network data to document constrained adaptation and household responses.
papers.conclusion: Adaptation is constrained in the short run, with frictions in labor adjustment.
papers.ident: Localized salinity shocks mapped from river salinity observations and canal network data, panel regressions
papers.dataDetail: River salinity observations, canal network data, household and firm data from the Mekong Delta

papers.title: Do black politicians matter? Political leadership and racial composition in top public sector positions

authors.inst: Escola de Economia de São Paulo
Escola de Economia de São Paulo

papers.q: Do Black politicians change the racial composition of top public sector positions in Brazil?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of how the race of political leaders affects the racial composition of top public sector appointments.

papers.title: Practical estimation methods for high-dimensional multivariate stochastic volatility models

authors.inst: Center for Interuniversity Research and Analysis on Organizations

papers.summary: The title indicates practical estimation methods for high-dimensional multivariate stochastic volatility models.

papers.title: Childbirth and Welfare Inequality: The Role of Bargaining Power and Intrahousehold Allocation
papers.q: How do bargaining power and intrahousehold allocation shape welfare inequality after childbirth?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of childbirth and welfare inequality through bargaining power and intrahousehold allocation.

papers.title: Labor Market Signals: The Role of Large Language Models
papers.q: How do large language models change the signals job seekers send through cover letters and recruiters' responses?
papers.summary: LLMs improve signal quality, especially for lower-quality applicants, but gains do not raise interview invitations because they concentrate in standardized, less influential sections. When recruiters learn of LLM use, they value high-quality, human-crafted letters more. A calibrated structural model suggests lower informativeness may increase matching inefficiencies.
papers.ident: Two field experiments on cover letters with and without LLM assistance and recruiter information; calibrated structural model
papers.contribution: Uses two field experiments to show LLM-assisted cover letters improve signal quality but reduce its informativeness.
papers.conclusion: LLMs reduce signal informativeness, potentially increasing inefficiencies in labor market matching.
papers.dataDetail: Cover letters and recruiter evaluations from field experiments

papers.title: Spillover Effects of Old-Age Pension across Generations: Family Labor Supply and Child Outcomes
papers.q: How does old-age pension spill over across generations to family labor supply and child outcomes?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of old-age pension spillovers to family labor supply and child outcomes.

papers.title: Specific Skills, Peer Effects, and Academic Outcomes: Evidence from Quasi-Randomly Assigned Roommates
papers.q: How do specific skills and peer effects shape academic outcomes among quasi-randomly assigned roommates?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of peer effects from specific skills on academic outcomes using quasi-random roommate assignment.

papers.title: Earnings Dynamics and Firm-Level Shocks
papers.q: How do firm-level shocks feed into workers' earnings dynamics?
papers.summary: The title indicates an analysis of earnings dynamics and firm-level shocks.

papers.title: An identification-and dimensionality-robust test for instrumental variables models
papers.summary: The test statistic has a limiting chi-squared distribution if an auxiliary parameter is consistently estimable, possible with machine learning even with more instruments than observations. A combination with the sup-score statistic improves power. First-stage F-statistics on LASSO-selected variables may be misleading, and performance is favorable in data and simulations.
papers.ident: New estimator and inference: identification-robust IV test using Lindeberg interpolation and machine learning
papers.contribution: Proposes an identification-robust test based on Lindeberg interpolation that works with many instruments, using machine learning for an auxiliary parameter.
papers.q: How can the structural parameter in a heteroskedastic IV model be tested robustly to weak identification when instruments outnumber observations?

papers.title: Rising inequality, declining mobility: The evolution of intergenerational mobility in Germany
papers.q: Has intergenerational income mobility in Germany declined across birth cohorts?
papers.summary: Intergenerational persistence for cohorts born 1968-1987 rises sharply for those born in the late 1970s and early 1980s, then stabilizes at a higher level. Parental income has become more important for children's educational outcomes. The rise coincided with a surge in cross-sectional inequality, an Intertemporal Great Gatsby Curve.
papers.ident: Descriptive: intergenerational income persistence by birth cohort, 1968-1987
papers.contribution: Provides the first evidence that German intergenerational income mobility has decreased, linking it to rising inequality.

papers.title: Matching Function Equilibria with Partial Assignment: Existence, Uniqueness and Estimation
papers.q: Do matching and discrete choice models share a common structure that guarantees existence, uniqueness and computation of equilibrium?
papers.summary: The structure combines an aggregate matching function and nonlinear equations. The paper offers an efficient algorithm and a counterfactual method needing no parametric estimation. It is applied to the 1982 elimination of the Social Security Student Benefit Program's effect on the US marriage market, comparing candidate models by information criterion.
papers.contribution: Defines matching function equilibria with partial assignment, proves existence and uniqueness, gives an algorithm and a parameter-free counterfactual approach.
papers.ident: New method: matching function equilibria with partial assignment; 1982 elimination of Social Security Student Benefit Program as application

papers.title: Relative affluence and mental health: Evidence from quasi-random class assignments

authors.inst: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

papers.q: Does relative affluence in a class affect students' mental health, using quasi-random class assignments?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of relative affluence and mental health with quasi-random class assignment.

papers.title: Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
papers.q: How are cognitive ability, risk preferences and decision errors related?
papers.summary: Intelligence has no impact on risk preferences but a robust link to errors.
papers.contribution: Builds a dataset of almost 260,000 decisions under risk by about 13,000 individuals with cognitive ability tests.
papers.conclusion: The results matter for theories of how cognitive ability affects decision making.
papers.ident: Estimation of risk preferences and error from decisions under risk, related to measured cognitive ability
papers.dataDetail: About 260,000 risky decisions by about 13,000 individuals with cognitive ability tests

papers.title: Will markets provide humane jobs?
papers.q: Why do laws rather than markets secure job amenities like sick leave, and when is a mandate optimal?
papers.summary: When workers who value an amenity are less productive, employers offering it attract a less productive workforce, so the compensating wage differential exceeds the direct cost and amenities are underprovided, even if costless, and markets may unravel. A mandate is optimal when the correlation is strong; policies leveraging observable heterogeneity do better when moderate.
papers.contribution: Formalizes adverse selection on productivity as a reason for underprovision of amenities, introducing the correlation in expectation.
papers.ident: Theory: competitive screening equilibrium with adverse selection on productivity and heterogeneous jobs

papers.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
papers.q: How do new products enter local markets through consumer social networks and retailer learning?
papers.summary: Expenditure shocks abroad transmitted via migrant networks shift which varieties consumers buy. Prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers or friends raise the likelihood of buying the same variety, especially premium and visible goods. Retailers add varieties to their assortment based on pioneer consumers' purchases.
papers.contribution: Matches customs records on individual direct-to-consumer imports with population-wide social networks and migrant links to identify demand externalities.
papers.ident: Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmitted through migrant networks as exogenous variation in local demand
papers.dataDetail: Customs records of individual imports, population-wide social networks, migrant links and retailer catchment areas

papers.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
papers.q: What is the optimal subsidy to flood insurance given fiscal spillovers, reclassification risk and moral hazard?
papers.summary: Moving the NFIP to actuarially fair premiums reduces insurance coverage, creating fiscal spillover onto FEMA aid and exposing households to uninsurable reclassification risk. The fiscal spillover and risk protection benefits significantly outweigh moral hazard costs, and the optimal subsidy is 51%, comparable to pre-reform levels.
papers.ident: Sufficient-statistics optimal insurance model with five parameters estimated via several identification strategies
papers.contribution: Develops a model of optimal flood insurance with static and dynamic tradeoffs and estimates its five key parameters using multiple identification strategies.

papers.title: Implementing an Optimal Tax Plan with Short Term Debt
papers.summary: Debt management in Lucas and Stokey (1983) fails to implement a Ramsey plan for flat-rate labor taxes when initial debt is too high. The proposed implementation equalizes Lagrange multipliers on the implementability constraints of the Ramsey and continuation planners, and is illustrated with different debt structures and spending patterns.
papers.q: Can short-term debt implement Ramsey optimal labor tax plans when initial government debt is high?
papers.contribution: Shows preventing continuation planners from resetting current taxes and financing deficits with short-term debt implements all Ramsey plans.
papers.ident: Theory: Ramsey plan implementation with short-term debt and continuation planners

papers.title: Welfare and the Act of Choosing
papers.q: How should welfare be evaluated when the act of choosing itself affects well-being?
papers.summary: The title suggests a welfare analysis that accounts for the act of choosing.

papers.title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
papers.q: How do population density, enclosure costs, productivity gains and governance capacity shape the privatization of land through decentralized enclosure?
papers.summary: Enclosure decisions may be strategic complements, generating tipping points and socially destructive property races, or substitutes, producing smoother transitions that may leave enclosure below the social optimum. Strengthening customary governance or compensating displaced stakeholders can realign incentives, but fixing one distortion while ignoring others can worsen welfare.
papers.contribution: Analyses enclosure with aggregative games, showing when decisions are strategic complements or substitutes and how policy distortions interact.
papers.ident: Theory: aggregative game of decentralized enclosure and property regimes

papers.title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information

authors.inst: Escola de Economia de São Paulo

papers.q: What is the robustly optimal way to combine correlated information sources when the correlation structure is unknown?
papers.summary: With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy uses only the best source and ignores the rest. With more actions, the problem decomposes into local comparisons each assigned to the best source, and with more states a concavification characterization assigns payoff-relevant components to best sources.
papers.conclusion: The results give a rationale for why ignoring information can be optimal and highlight benefits of specialized sources when correlations are ambiguous.
papers.contribution: Characterizes strategies maximizing worst-case payoff guarantees across all correlation structures.
papers.ident: Theory: robust decision problem with worst-case guarantee across correlation structures

papers.title: Modeling and Evaluating the Labor Market and Fiscal Effects of Immigration

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.summary: The welfare effect on natives of a one-percentage-point inflow varies in sign and size, depending on immigrant skill mix, wage gaps, unemployment and tax progressivity. For inflows matching 2019-2024 arrivals, native welfare rises in 14 of 17 economies. Lower-skilled natives gain from higher pre-tax earnings, higher-skilled natives from lower labor-tax burdens.
papers.conclusion: Evaluating immigration policy requires modeling labor market and fiscal channels jointly.
papers.ident: Calibrated general-equilibrium model with search frictions, skill-specific taxes and public goods, 17 OECD countries
papers.contribution: Builds a general-equilibrium search-and-matching model with progressive taxes and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries.
papers.q: What are the combined labor market and fiscal effects of immigration on native welfare across OECD countries?
papers.dataDetail: Calibration to 17 OECD countries, 2015-2019

papers.title: Venture Capital and Customer Capital
papers.summary: VC finances firms with higher sales and marketing spending, wage bills and trademark applications more than other intermediaries. VCs target high-customer-capital, low-knowledge-capital industries. Firms tilt investment toward customer capital before the first VC investment and scale rapidly afterward. Spray-and-pray VCs target customer capital industries; concentrated VCs target knowledge capital industries.
papers.contribution: Documents VC's focus on customer capital rather than knowledge capital and explains it by power-law returns and risk tolerance.
papers.q: Why does venture capital specialize in financing customer-capital-intensive firms?
papers.ident: Descriptive: VC investment patterns by firm and industry customer capital and knowledge capital intensity
papers.dataDetail: Firm-level sales and marketing expense, trademark applications and venture capital investment data

papers.title: Home-Foreign Elasticity Functions and the Gains from Trade
papers.summary: Estimated home-foreign elasticities generally rise with domestic expenditure shares across WIOD and OECD ICIO data. In a multi-sector model with intermediate inputs, the median WIOD country gain is 19.37 log points versus 24.43 with fixed initial elasticities.
papers.q: How can gains from trade be calculated without assuming a constant trade elasticity?
papers.contribution: Derives gains from trade for general homothetic preferences using home-foreign elasticity functions and estimates them nonparametrically from trade agreement tariff changes.
papers.ident: Nonparametric identification of home-foreign elasticity functions from tariff changes implied by trade agreements
papers.dataDetail: WIOD and OECD ICIO input-output data; tariff changes from trade agreements

papers.title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
papers.summary: The why asks which problems to tackle and who benefits, recipients, donors or global public goods. The how asks which strategy is cost-effective, using and producing evidence. Approaches improving state capacity to use and generate evidence serve several objectives, and the how is iterative.
papers.conclusion: Learning, adapting and sharing evidence iteratively is central to the how of aid.
papers.q: What motivates foreign aid and which strategies deliver it most cost-effectively?
papers.contribution: Separates the why and the how of aid to clarify real and false tensions, stressing evidence and state capacity.
papers.ident: Descriptive: conceptual and review essay on foreign aid

papers.title: Understanding Migration Responses to Local Shocks
papers.q: How should migration regressions of population changes on local labor demand shocks be interpreted?
papers.summary: Common conclusions from migration regression estimates are likely misleading. The regression is inaccurate for within-sample effects of observed shocks and uninformative for counterfactual shocks, especially with industry switching costs. Analytical results and simulations on Brazilian data support this.
papers.ident: Theory and simulation: local labor market model with mobility costs, evaluating migration regression estimands
papers.contribution: Shows in a model with mobility costs that conventional migration regressions are misspecified because they omit shocks to alternative locations.
papers.dataDetail: Brazilian data for simulations

papers.title: Correcting for Heterogeneity in the Use of Subjective Scales
papers.q: How can survey analyses correct for heterogeneity in how respondents use subjective scales?
papers.summary: In new data (N about 10,000) and existing data, the mapping between respondents' scales is approximately linear. The estimator is validated with ratings of height and weight and illustrated with life satisfaction regressions, where correction leaves qualitative findings intact but can substantially change coefficient ratios, tripling the estimated cost of unemployment relative to income.
papers.ident: New estimator: scale-use-corrected regressions using calibration questions such as vignettes
papers.contribution: Formalizes calibration-question (vignette) correction theory and develops a simple estimator based on approximately linear scale mappings.
papers.dataDetail: New survey of about 10,000 respondents and existing data

papers.title: Credit Markets with New Screening Technologies

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.q: How do new screening technologies, including correlated AI screening errors, shape credit market structure?
papers.summary: With independent errors a single segment emerges with rates rising smoothly. With correlated errors, ex-ante identical lenders specialize across distinct segments, generating a hockey-stick rate schedule echoing banking, fintech and high-rate lending. Changes in screening costs, including AI and open banking, unevenly affect access and can help or harm excluded borrowers.
papers.contribution: Models credit competition with endogenous screening and a pool externality from rejected borrowers reapplying elsewhere.
papers.ident: Theory: credit market competition model with endogenous screening technologies and correlated errors

papers.title: From Politics to Process: Evidence from Progressive Era Naturalizations
papers.q: Do federal standards for citizenship adjudication discipline politically biased administration, as in the 1906 Naturalization Act?
papers.summary: Standardization led to rapid convergence of naturalization practices across cities. Naturalizations were about 30% higher in election years before the reform, but this cycle disappeared, most strongly in cities without civil service reforms. Affected cohorts earned 7% more, entered citizenship-restricted occupations more and gave children more Americanized names.
papers.conclusion: Standardizing administrative procedures can discipline politically biased implementation.
papers.ident: Event study around the 1906 Naturalization Act; staggered municipal civil service reforms
papers.contribution: Uses newly digitized census records on over five million immigrants to show standardization removed electoral cycles in naturalization.
papers.dataDetail: Newly digitized census records covering over five million immigrants over 30 years

papers.title: Are We Consuming Too Much Groundwater?
papers.q: Are the world's aquifers being depleted faster than is optimal?
papers.summary: Three- to four-fifths of aquifers are extracted too rapidly, decreasing present value by several percent and creating trillions of dollars in welfare losses. Policies guaranteeing constant quantities indefinitely, or fully discounting future extraction, generate larger welfare costs. A sustainable path maintaining current fill lowers welfare, as most stocks are already too low.
papers.ident: Dynamic extraction model per aquifer, recovering the discount factor that rationalizes observed extraction, benchmarked to Ramsey and market paths
papers.contribution: Estimates a dynamic extraction model for each of many aquifers using remote sensing data and compares with Ramsey and market benchmarks.
papers.dataDetail: Remote sensing and economic data for many of the world's 3,400 aquifers

papers.title: Too Little too Late? Nationwide Carbon Trading in China
papers.summary: High-efficiency power plants raised generation and CO2 emissions by about 5% relative to low-efficiency plants, with no clear differential reduction in emission intensity. Against Indonesian and Philippine coal plants, China's high-efficiency plants also increased emissions. Air quality worsened downwind of high-efficiency plants.
papers.contribution: Provides first empirical evidence on a rate-based carbon market using satellite imagery and machine learning plant-level data.
papers.q: How did China's rate-based nationwide carbon market affect plant-level generation, emissions and air quality?
papers.ident: Differential responses by plant efficiency after the 2021 launch, plus comparison with coal plants in countries without carbon markets
papers.dataDetail: Plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning

papers.title: Export Controls and the Economics of National Security
papers.q: How effective are export controls at restricting adversaries' access to military-relevant goods, and how does multilateralism matter?
papers.summary: Controls impose large export and entry frictions, substantially smaller for exports to multilateral regime members, equal to 15-29 log points of export cost. Only 7% of the reduction in controlled exports is replaced by other countries under multilateral controls versus 28% under unilateral US policy. Multilateral controls raise adversaries' military price index and the US's relative real military expenditure by about 1 log point versus 0.14.
papers.ident: Quantitative GE model with dual-use production and input-output linkages, estimated using US export control classification and licensing data
papers.contribution: Combines new data on US export control classifications and licensing with a quantitative GE model with dual-use production.
papers.dataDetail: US export control classifications and licensing outcomes

papers.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
papers.q: Why are some firms more likely than others to sponsor workers' skills training?
papers.summary: Better managed firms, even within industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, and training clusters around managerial or frontline development. Organizational differences give firms incentives to train beyond labor market frictions by making general skills firm-specific.
papers.contribution: Documents that better-managed firms train more and links training to organizational heterogeneity in a knowledge hierarchy framework.
papers.ident: Descriptive evidence on firm training and management practices, interpreted with a knowledge hierarchy model

papers.title: The Long March to Innovation: R&D and Competitive Evolution in the Indian Pharmaceutical Industry
papers.summary: Using Biomedtracker trial data benchmarked against China and the UK, the Indian pipeline faces a bottleneck in moving trials from Phase 1 to Phase 2, with a null result for Phase 1 to Phase 3 transitions. Binding constraints likely unrelated to IPR, with a within-firm shift to non-novel programs, supported by expert interviews.
papers.conclusion: Findings should inform normative thinking on IPR in developing economies.
papers.ident: Descriptive: clinical trial phase transition rates benchmarked against China and the UK, plus expert interviews
papers.contribution: Uses trial phase transition data to show a Phase 1 to Phase 2 bottleneck and argues it is orthogonal to intellectual property rights.
papers.q: Why has the Indian pharmaceutical innovation pipeline stalled two decades after TRIPS?
papers.dataDetail: Biomedtracker clinical trial phase transition data; interviews with industry experts

papers.title: Green Subsidies with Demand Distortions
papers.q: How do credit constraints and other demand distortions change the welfare gains from green subsidies for clean cookstoves in Kenya?
papers.summary: Among 2,134 Kenyan charcoal users, 75% usage subsidies have a precise zero effect, while purchase price subsidies generate large welfare gains. Credit constraints raise subsidy efficacy by 35%-73% and lower the abatement subsidy cost by 41% to US$12 per tCO2e; without demand distortions it would be US$137.
papers.contribution: Models clean technology adoption with demand distortions and tests it by cross-randomizing purchase subsidies, usage subsidies and interest-free loans.
papers.ident: Cross-randomized purchase price subsidies, usage subsidies and interest-free loan access for an induction stove, 2,134 charcoal users
papers.dataDetail: Field experiment with 2,134 charcoal users in Kenya

papers.title: Inside Central Bankers’ Calendars: How Do Fed Chairs Allocate Their Time?
papers.q: How do Federal Reserve Chairs allocate their time across meetings with staff, media and lawmakers?
papers.summary: All three Chairs spend more than 30% of documented meetings with Fed staff. Media interactions rose under Bernanke and stayed important through Powell's tenure, and Powell met lawmakers significantly more than his predecessors. Time allocation also responds to business cycle shifts, placed in historical context with Greenspan's calendars.
papers.contribution: Constructs a novel dataset of more than 20,000 daily calendar entries of Bernanke, Yellen and Powell.
papers.ident: Descriptive: time allocation patterns in Fed Chairs' daily calendars, and business cycle responses
papers.dataDetail: More than 20,000 calendar entries of three Federal Reserve Chairs

papers.title: A Model of U.S. Monetary Policy and the Global Financial Cycle
papers.q: How does US monetary policy affect global risk premia through currency-mismatched arbitrageurs?
papers.summary: Assuming mean-variance efficient portfolios, arbitrageurs must be short the dollar, so a US tightening revalues their wealth downward. The mechanism is disciplined to match effects of US policy on international asset prices, and used to quantify macro spillovers and policy responses abroad. With higher dollar rates, arbitrageurs' dollar funding and spillovers are dampened.
papers.ident: Theory and quantification: general equilibrium model with currency-mismatched arbitrageurs matched to asset price responses
papers.contribution: Proposes a general equilibrium model where US tightening erodes dollar-short arbitrageurs' net worth, raising the global price of risk.

papers.title: The Robust Properties of Economies with Endogenous Production Networks
papers.summary: The min reflects resilience from supplier substitution and the max fragility from complementarity-induced rigidity. Local Domar weights are generally insufficient to describe even small shocks' propagation, and smooth changes in Domar weights overstate microeconomic volatility's adverse effect on GDP by omitting option value of switching suppliers.
papers.ident: Theory: equilibrium characterization of endogenous production network economies
papers.q: What are the robust properties of equilibria in economies with endogenous production networks?
papers.contribution: Characterizes log-prices as a min-max over networks of an affine function of log-productivities and generalizes Hulten's theorem.

papers.title: Investment irreversibility in a granular world
papers.summary: Irreversibility dampens volatility of output, investment and hours while amplifying consumption volatility. Eliminating the friction yields a 1.83% consumption-equivalent welfare gain, but subsidizing capital liquidation reduces welfare by 0.59%, since compensated firms over-disinvest.
papers.q: Does investment irreversibility matter for aggregate fluctuations in an economy with large, fat-tailed-distributed firms?
papers.contribution: Shows irreversibility shapes aggregate fluctuations in a granular economy through misallocation and general equilibrium channels.
papers.ident: Quantitative heterogeneous-firm model with fat-tailed firm size distribution and investment irreversibility

papers.title: Does trade exposure explain anti-globalization votes?

authors.inst: Centre d'Etudes Prospectives et d'Informations Internationales
Centre d'Etudes Prospectives et d'Informations Internationales
Centre d'Etudes Prospectives et d'Informations Internationales

papers.q: Does exposure to trade and immigration explain anti-globalization voting in France?
papers.summary: Import competition increases anti-globalization voting and export exposure reduces it, in line with local employment effects. Immigration also raises such voting. Final goods imports increase it while intermediate goods imports reduce it, as they support domestic employment within global value chains.
papers.contribution: Builds a novel measure of anti-globalization voting combining presidential candidates' manifesto positions with local election outcomes.
papers.ident: Local trade and immigration exposure measures regressed on anti-globalization vote share, France 1988-2022
papers.dataDetail: Presidential candidate manifestos, local electoral outcomes, trade flows, France 1988-2022

papers.title: Contracting Structures in Public Procurement: Evidence from Donor-Funded Electrification in Kenya

authors.n: Hsu, Eric ; Miguel, Edward ; Ochieng, Eric ; Walker, Michael

papers.q: How do contracting and monitoring structures in public procurement affect infrastructure construction quality and speed in Kenya?
papers.summary: World Bank-funded contracts featured unbundled design-bid-build components and enhanced monitoring compared to African Development Bank contracts. Unbundling delayed construction but improved quality. Randomized inspections improved quality without large delays.
papers.contribution: Leverages natural and experimental variation and independent construction quality data from Kenya Power's donor-funded electrification contracts.
papers.conclusion: Bundled contracting with additional independent monitoring could improve outcomes.
papers.ident: Natural variation across donor-funded contract types and randomized inspections of construction quality
papers.dataDetail: Kenya Power procurement contracts and independently collected construction quality data

papers.title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
papers.q: Do women respond more than men to treatments in experimental economics?
papers.summary: Neither analysis finds that gender predicts responsiveness to treatment. Over two hundred pairwise tests using two studies find the same. The hypothesis is referenced predominantly by papers that support it.
papers.contribution: Tests the female sensitivity hypothesis across over two hundred experimental papers and two datasets.
papers.ident: Meta-analysis of over two hundred experimental papers and over two hundred pairwise tests in two studies
papers.dataDetail: Experimental economics papers; data from DellaVigna and Pope (2022) and Exley et al. (2025)

papers.title: Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
papers.q: How do parents respond to fetal shocks like Ramadan fasting during pregnancy, and how does the macroeconomy matter?
papers.summary: Children exposed to Ramadan fasting in utero have lower full vaccination rates for DPT and polio than non-exposed siblings. Parents compensate during booms and reinforce during downturns. The estimates imply about half a million excess infant deaths over three decades.
papers.contribution: Uses 150 DHS surveys in 50 countries and sibling comparisons to study parental compensation or reinforcement of fetal shocks.
papers.ident: Sibling comparisons of in-utero exposure to Ramadan fasting, interacted with macroeconomic conditions
papers.dataDetail: 150 Demographic and Health Surveys from 50 developing countries

papers.title: Does the United States spend enough on public schools? Evidence from a market-based efficiency test
papers.q: Does the United States spend enough on public schools, as tested by the response of house prices to tax-funded school spending?
papers.summary: School spending is efficient if a locally tax-funded increase would leave house prices unchanged. Using 25 years of national local house price data, an exogenous tax-funded spending increase would significantly raise house prices.
papers.conclusion: Teacher spending in the US is inefficiently low.
papers.ident: Spatial equilibrium test of capitalization using plausibly exogenous shocks to school spending and taxes
papers.contribution: Provides a market-based efficiency test using a spatial equilibrium model and exogenous shocks to spending and taxes.
papers.dataDetail: 25 years of national data on local house prices, school spending and taxes

papers.title: Detecting tariff evasion: Evidence from matched container data

authors.inst: Centre d'Etudes Prospectives et d'Informations Internationales

papers.q: Can matched container data detect tariff evasion?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of detecting tariff evasion using matched container data.

papers.title: How do firms respond to parental leave absences?
papers.q: How do firms adjust labor demand when a female employee takes parental leave?
papers.summary: Firms respond mainly through anticipatory hiring, with small medium-run effects on employment and wage bill. Replacement hiring is female, but the workforce shifts toward men in the medium run, driven by shorter tenure of female new hires and higher male incumbent retention. Longer leave extends absences but not systematically labor demand responses.
papers.contribution: Compares Austrian firms with and without a birth event and exploits reforms that changed leave durations.
papers.conclusion: Firms accommodate leave mainly through anticipatory hiring and gendered composition changes, with limited medium-run changes in aggregate labor demand.
papers.ident: Event study comparing firms with and without a birth event, exploiting Austrian parental leave reforms
papers.dataDetail: Austrian administrative employer-employee data

papers.title: How Credible Are the Findings from Online Experiments?
papers.q: How credible are published results from online experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk?
papers.summary: There is evidence of widespread p-hacking, publication bias and underpowered studies, varying across fields: marketing is badly afflicted with little distortion in economics. Online and laboratory results from the same outlets show similar distortions, with bunching above the significance threshold more pronounced on MTurk.
papers.ident: Meta-analysis of test statistics from MTurk experiments, p-hacking and publication bias diagnostics
papers.contribution: Examines the universe of MTurk hypotheses reported in leading journals from 2010 to 2021 for p-hacking and publication bias.
papers.dataDetail: All hypotheses tested on Amazon Mechanical Turk in leading journals, 2010-2021

papers.title: A Theory of Economic Coercion and Fragmentation

papers.summary: The title suggests a theory of economic coercion and fragmentation.

papers.title: Gas flaring, agricultural productivity and labor reallocation: Evidence from Nigeria
papers.q: How does natural gas flaring affect agricultural productivity and labor in southern Nigeria?
papers.summary: Gas flaring has significant negative effects on crop yield per hectare and labor productivity during the harvest season, particularly in rainy periods, with minimal effects during planting. The strategy uses survey timing variation, fixed effects, weather controls and a 2010 Local Content Act reform.
papers.ident: IV using global oil price changes interacted with pre-sample flaring intensity; household and region-month-year fixed effects; survey timing
papers.contribution: Combines LSMS household panel data with geocoded monthly flaring volumes and an IV based on oil prices and pre-sample flaring intensity.
papers.dataDetail: Nigerian LSMS household panel 2012-2018; geocoded monthly gas flaring volumes

papers.title: Structural transformation towards healthcare
papers.q: How does structural transformation toward healthcare unfold?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of structural transformation toward the healthcare sector.

papers.title: Love-for-variety: with an application to an Armington model of competitive trade
papers.q: How can love-for-variety be defined and applied in an Armington model of competitive trade?
papers.summary: The title indicates a treatment of love-for-variety with an application to an Armington model of competitive trade.
papers.ident: Theory: love-for-variety in demand systems

papers.title: Closing Ranks: Organized Labor and Immigration
papers.q: How does organized labor respond to immigration?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of organized labor's response to immigration.

papers.title: Conflict or Compromise? Theory and Evidence from Africa and Asia
papers.q: Why don't leaders in weak states share power to avoid civil conflict?
papers.summary: Power sharing makes challengers more effective at rebelling, so commitment worsens as the opposition strengthens. As challengers become stronger, inclusion increases up to a threshold, beyond which the leader excludes them and faces conflict. Empirical findings on politically relevant ethnic groups strongly accord with the predictions.
papers.contribution: Models a commitment problem in power sharing, tests its non-monotonic implications on ethnic groups in Africa and Asia, and estimates it structurally.
papers.ident: Within-country variation in ethnic group population share as proxy for group strength; structural estimation of the model
papers.dataDetail: Politically relevant ethnic groups, access to executive power, armed organizations in Africa and Asia

papers.title: Trade, Human Capital, and Income Risk,
papers.q: How does trade exposure affect individual income risk, and how does human capital condition it?
papers.summary: Imports increase income risk and exports decrease it. Workers with more industry- or occupation-specific human capital face lower risk on average, but net imports raise risk more for workers with longer industry tenure, with small mean income effects. Welfare consequences are dominated by the risk channel.
papers.contribution: Uses worker-level longitudinal data from Germany to causally link industry trade exposure to income risk and builds a welfare framework combining mean and risk.
papers.ident: Industry trade exposure measures related to worker income risk, Germany 1976-2012
papers.dataDetail: Worker-level longitudinal data from Germany, 1976-2012

papers.title: Investment-goods market power and capital accumulation
papers.q: How does market power in investment goods affect capital accumulation?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of investment-goods market power and capital accumulation.

papers.title: Buying Data from Consumers: The Impact of Monitoring in U.S. Auto Insurance
papers.q: What is the impact of consumer monitoring on US auto insurance, where firms buy data from consumers?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of buying data from consumers through monitoring in US auto insurance.

papers.title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Impact of Immigration: Evidence from German Establishments
papers.q: How does firm heterogeneity shape the impact of immigration in German establishments?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of immigration's effects with firm heterogeneity using German establishment data.
papers.dataDetail: German establishment data

papers.title: Immigration and the Slope of the Labour Demand Curve: The Role of Firm Heterogeneity in a Model of Regional Labour Markets
papers.q: Why do migrants not decrease natives' wages, and why can skilled immigration raise them?
papers.summary: Skilled immigration induces skill-intensive firms to expand, which reduces within-firm substitution between skilled and unskilled workers and limits relative wage adjustment. With skill-neutral firm-level but skill-biased aggregate human capital externalities, skilled immigration can raise absolute and relative skilled wages. Across-firm reallocation reduces negative wage effects by at least one-third.
papers.ident: Theory: regional labour market model with heterogeneous firms, imperfectly substitutable skills and human capital externalities, quantified
papers.contribution: Develops a regional labour market model with heterogeneous firms showing how across-firm reallocation and human capital externalities shape wage effects.

papers.title: Capturing international influences in U.S. monetary policy through a Natural Language Processing approach
papers.q: How can international influences on US monetary policy be captured with natural language processing?
papers.summary: The title suggests an NLP approach to measuring international influences in US monetary policy.

papers.title: Measurement Error in Self-Reported Data on Stigmatized Behavior: Experimental Evidence on Intimate Partner Violence

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.summary: Improved privacy yields higher and more accurate IPV reports than both standard surveys and list experiments, especially among women with low education. Linking data with two natural experiments shows that non-random underreporting can bias estimates of IPV determinants.
papers.ident: Randomized comparison of ballot, standard survey and list experiment reporting methods, linked with two natural experiments
papers.contribution: Introduces a privacy-enhancing ballot method and compares it with standard surveys and list experiments.
papers.q: How does privacy in data collection affect measured intimate partner violence?
papers.dataDetail: Survey data on intimate partner violence with experimental reporting modes

papers.title: How Knowledge Crosses Borders: Evidence from Semiconductor Manufacturing

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research
Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.summary: Cross-border learning is important in modern semiconductor manufacturing, and several channels operate through purposeful economic relationships.
papers.conclusion: Access to frontier knowledge is neither automatic nor guaranteed, so domestic technological upgrading policies work best with continued access to global frontier knowledge.
papers.ident: Descriptive: channels of cross-border knowledge diffusion in semiconductor manufacturing
papers.q: How does knowledge cross borders in semiconductor manufacturing?
papers.contribution: Shows cross-border learning operates through market mechanisms such as supply chains, engineer movement and FDI rather than anonymous spillovers.

papers.title: Affirmative Action in Centralized College Admissions Systems
papers.q: What are the overall equilibrium effects of affirmative action in centralized college admissions on benefited and displaced students?
papers.summary: Marginally benefited targeted students attend and graduate from higher-quality programs, with graduation gains about twice marginally displaced students' losses. Among all reallocated students, benefited students gain nearly twice what displaced lose, but equilibrium reallocations displace about 30% more students than benefited, so non-targeted losses offset about two-thirds of gains.
papers.conclusion: The policy leaves a modest net gain in graduation across all students.
papers.contribution: Develops a framework separating marginal effects from overall equilibrium reallocation effects and applies it to Brazil's federal quota law.
papers.ident: Admissions cutoff RDD for marginal students, plus structural model of degree choices and potential outcomes
papers.dataDetail: Brazilian centralized college admissions and graduation records

papers.title: When Cash Flows Turn Negative: Liquidity-Driven Selling by Pension Funds
papers.q: Do US public pension funds with negative cash flows act as stabilizing, contrarian investors or as liquidity-driven equity sellers?
papers.summary: Pension funds with more negative cash flows do not adjust target allocations and keep low safe-asset buffers, so they meet cash flow shocks mainly by selling equities, absorbing $0.67 per dollar of shock. They sell across equities and even when equity returns are negative, reflecting liquidity needs rather than rebalancing.
papers.conclusion: Pension funds have become regular equity sellers rather than contrarian, stabilizing investors.
papers.contribution: Combines aggregate public pension data with granular holdings from public records requests to show pensions meet cash shocks by selling equities.
papers.ident: Regressions of equity sales on pension fund cash flow shocks, using aggregate and security-level holdings
papers.dataDetail: Aggregate US public pension data and granular holdings from public records requests

papers.title: What Can (and Cannot) Be Learned about Systemic Racial Discrimination from Randomized Controlled Trials?
papers.q: Can randomized controlled trials reveal systemic racial discrimination, as opposed to direct discrimination?
papers.summary: The essay considers seven approaches: large-scale manipulation, smaller-scale designs, trials across structural settings, salience of systemic forces, information, salience of racial identity, and strategic responses. It also points to other approaches that fill gaps left by RCTs.
papers.ident: Descriptive: conceptual essay on RCT-based study of systemic racial discrimination
papers.contribution: Proposes a conceptual model of systemic racial discrimination and assesses possibilities and limits of RCTs for studying it.

papers.title: The Relationship between Income and Health: Evidence from Nationwide Health Exams in Korea
papers.q: How do physical health, health behaviors and mortality vary with income among prime-age Koreans?
papers.summary: For both sexes, disease-income gradients are negative for high blood pressure, glucose and BMI but not cholesterol, steeper for women, and concentrated in the top half of the income distribution. Mortality-income gradients are also concentrated in the top half but steeper for men. Differences in health measures explain very little of the income-mortality gradient.
papers.conclusion: Something other than prime-age disease burden differences drives most of the income-mortality gradient at older ages.
papers.contribution: Links population-wide cardiovascular health exams to income tax records and mortality for about 350,000 Koreans aged 47-57.
papers.ident: Descriptive: income gradients in health measures and mortality from linked health exams, tax records and mortality data
papers.dataDetail: Korean nationwide cardiovascular health exams linked to income tax records and mortality, about 350,000 people

papers.title: Inflation, households, and central banks around the world
papers.q: How do households and central banks around the world respond to inflation?
papers.summary: The title suggests an international analysis of inflation, households and central banks.

papers.title: Feasible GLS for time series regression
papers.q: How can feasible generalized least squares be applied to time series regression?
papers.summary: The title indicates work on feasible GLS for time series regression.
papers.ident: Theory: feasible GLS estimation in time series regression

papers.title: Too little too late? Nationwide carbon trading in China
papers.summary: High-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO2 emissions by about 5% relative to low-efficiency plants, with no clear differential reduction in emission intensity. Relative to Indonesian and Philippine coal plants, China's high-efficiency plants also increased emissions. Air quality worsened downwind of high-efficiency plants.
papers.contribution: Provides the first empirical evidence on a rate-based carbon market using satellite imagery and machine learning plant-level data.
papers.q: How did China's rate-based nationwide carbon market affect plant-level generation, emissions and air quality?
papers.ident: Differential responses by plant efficiency after the 2021 launch, plus comparison with coal plants in countries without carbon markets
papers.dataDetail: Plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning

papers.title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
papers.q: How does online job search advice affect job seekers' outcomes, directly and through spillovers?
papers.summary: Advice significantly increases employment and earnings when given to a limited share of job seekers, but effects diminish and disappear as treatment intensity rises, due to negative spillovers among treated job seekers and congestion in occupations they redirect to. Spillovers on untreated seekers are heterogeneous.
papers.ident: Two-stage randomized field experiment with regionally varying treatment intensity providing vacancy information and occupational recommendations
papers.contribution: Uses a two-stage randomized design with regionally varying treatment intensity on the Danish public employment service platform.
papers.dataDetail: Danish public employment service online platform and administrative data

papers.title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
papers.q: How does quality regulation of generic drugs through bioequivalence affect competition and welfare?
papers.summary: Stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs by 18% and raised average paid prices by 13%. Regulation increased demand for generics by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, inducing entry of high-quality drugs over low-quality ones. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and fewer firms.
papers.contribution: Exploits Chile's introduction of bioequivalence requirements and estimates a model of drug entry, certification and demand.
papers.ident: Introduction of bioequivalence requirements in Chile, with a structural model of entry, certification and demand
papers.dataDetail: Chilean pharmaceutical market data

papers.title: A trade-off between monetary policy transmission and systemic risk
papers.q: Is there a trade-off between monetary policy transmission and systemic risk?
papers.summary: The title suggests an analysis of a trade-off between monetary policy transmission and systemic risk.

papers.title: Massive Open Online Courses and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from Colombia
papers.q: Do MOOC certificates improve labor market outcomes in Colombia?
papers.summary: Only 6.2% of eligible participants completed a course. MOOC certificates raise formal employment by about 5 percentage points, with larger effects for those not employed at baseline and low-income households, no clear gender differences, and gains concentrated in larger firms and sectors aligned with the course.
papers.ident: Event study of certificate receipt, with randomized eligibility for free Coursera certificates
papers.contribution: Uses a Coursera initiative offering free certificates during COVID-19, with randomized eligibility and an event-study design due to low completion.
papers.conclusion: MOOCs can improve employment, but additional interventions appear necessary to raise completion rates.
papers.dataDetail: Coursera participation data linked to Colombian formal employment records

papers.title: Are Markups Too High? Competition, Strategic Innovation, and Industry Dynamics
papers.q: Are markups too high, given competition, strategic innovation and industry dynamics?
papers.summary: Within each industry an endogenous number of superstar firms compete à la Cournot alongside small fringe firms, with endogenous innovation, entry and exit. The model is consistent with US trends since the 1970s: domination by superstar firms, higher markups, concentration, profits and R&D, and lower dynamism, productivity growth and labour share.
papers.contribution: Develops an oligopolistic general-equilibrium Schumpeterian growth model with superstar firms and a competitive fringe.
papers.ident: Structural estimation of an oligopolistic Schumpeterian growth model
papers.dataDetail: US industry and firm data

papers.title: Human capital accumulation across space
papers.q: How does human capital accumulate across locations, and how does this shape the spatial distribution of economic activity?
papers.summary: Studies how human capital accumulation varies across space.

papers.title: Household liquidity and the adjustable-rate mortgage cash-flow channel of monetary policy
papers.q: How does household liquidity shape the transmission of monetary policy through adjustable-rate mortgage cash flows?
papers.summary: Studies how household liquidity governs the adjustable-rate mortgage cash-flow channel of monetary policy.

papers.title: Crowding Out Temptation: Experimental Evidence on Savings and Health Behaviors in Kenya
papers.q: Can a lottery-linked savings intervention reduce spending on alcohol, transactional sex and gambling and improve health outcomes in Kenya?
papers.summary: Over 24 months, the savings intervention raised formal savings and assets, financed mainly by lower spending on alcohol, transactional sex and gambling. Hazardous drinking fell by 26% and intimate partner violence by 15%; HIV/STI incidence fell by 8%, not statistically significant.
papers.conclusion: Savings interventions can simultaneously boost financial security and change health behaviour.
papers.ident: Randomized controlled trial of a lottery-based savings intervention in Kenya, followed over 24 months.
papers.contribution: Provides randomized evidence that a savings product combining lottery-based interest, goal-setting and reminders shifts spending away from temptation goods and improves health behaviours.
papers.dataDetail: RCT data from Kenya over 24 months

papers.title: Does Food Assistance Drive Spending on Sugary Foods? Evidence from the Pandemic Electronic Benefit Transfer Program
papers.summary: P-EBT disbursement raised weekly spending on sugary items by 16% among SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children, more than the rise in their overall food spending. No changes appear among households unlikely to receive benefits or in placebo years.
papers.conclusion: Households allocated a disproportionate share of P-EBT-driven purchases to sugary items relative to their baseline, relevant to proposals restricting SNAP purchases of high-sugar items.
papers.ident: Stacked difference-in-differences exploiting state-level variation in the timing of P-EBT disbursements, with placebo years.
papers.contribution: Provides causal evidence on food assistance and sugary purchases using the staggered state rollout of Pandemic EBT benefits and NielsenIQ scanner data.
papers.q: Does food assistance raise spending on sugary foods among low-income households with school-aged children?
papers.dataDetail: NielsenIQ Consumer Panel household purchase data

papers.title: Targeted Acceleration in Middle School Math: Impacts on College Entry, Degree Completion, and STEM
papers.q: How does admission to an accelerated middle school math program affect college entry, degree completion and STEM majors, by non-cognitive skill and gender?
papers.summary: Marginally eligible boys with high non-cognitive skills are 33 percentage points more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade and 12 points more likely to complete a STEM or business major within 6 years; low non-cognitive boys see no college gains. High non-cognitive girls are 17 points more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade.
papers.contribution: Uses a test-score cutoff for an accelerated math track to estimate long-run college effects, showing they depend sharply on non-cognitive skills and gender.
papers.ident: Regression discontinuity at the 80th-percentile 5th-grade math score cutoff for program entry in a large urban district.
papers.dataDetail: Student records from a large urban US school district, followed six years after high school

papers.title: Soft Reserves, Learning and Bid Adjustment in Advertising Auctions
papers.q: Can advertisers learn through repeated bidding that a nominally second-price auction uses soft reserves, and what are the welfare effects of adjustment?
papers.summary: If each charge equal to the bid is flagged, soft reserves are exposed quickly; if reports show only win rates and expected charges, they are indistinguishable from a second-price auction at any fixed bid. Among informed symmetric advertisers, soft reserves raise no more revenue than a second-price auction, and partial adjustment misallocates placements.
papers.conclusion: The second-price description and aggregate reporting act as complements in hiding soft reserves.
papers.contribution: Models learning by advertisers facing undisclosed soft reserves, motivated by the FTC allegations against Amazon, and shows aggregate reporting can make them undetectable.
papers.ident: Theory: repeated auction model with Bayesian learning by advertisers about soft reserves.

papers.title: Propensity to consume food out of SNAP and its welfare implications
papers.q: How much of SNAP benefits do recipients spend on food, and what does this imply for welfare?
papers.summary: Studies the marginal propensity to consume food out of SNAP benefits and its welfare implications.

papers.title: Aging Out of Coverage: Lessons from the West Virginia $1,000 Adult Dental Benefit

authors.inst: Pacific Northwest University of Health Sciences

papers.q: How did West Virginia's adult Medicaid dental benefit change dental care use at the age-21 coverage threshold, and does provider supply matter?
papers.summary: Before the benefit, quarterly use of preventive and restorative dental services fell from 8% at age 20 to almost 0% at 21; afterwards it fell only to 5%, a net increase of 50% of baseline. Effects are significantly larger in counties with more oral health provider practices.
papers.conclusion: Public health insurance expansions are dampened in markets with limited provider supply.
papers.contribution: Exploits the drop in Medicaid dental coverage at age 21 before and after a new $1,000 adult benefit to estimate utilization effects and their dependence on provider supply.
papers.ident: Age-21 coverage discontinuity compared before and after implementation of West Virginia's adult Medicaid dental benefit.
papers.dataDetail: West Virginia Medicaid dental claims data

papers.title: Aligning Platform and User Incentives in Social Media Age Restrictions
papers.q: Can a regulatory regime with a platform-provided safe tier for teens achieve better adherence and welfare than outright social media age bans?
papers.summary: Offering a safe tier without features such as algorithmic feeds complements enforcement: teens can comply without losing their network, and platforms retain displaced users as lower-margin customers. The design makes teens' choice to avoid the adult tier less dependent on peer dynamics and raises teen welfare for a relevant range of penalties.
papers.contribution: Proposes and models a regulatory design where platforms stay liable for teens on the adult tier but may offer a restricted safe tier preserving network interactions.
papers.ident: Theory: model of platform and teen choices with network effects under alternative age-restriction regimes.

papers.title: Optimal Line-Drawing for Legal Rules
papers.summary: Optimal thresholds are characterized generally and for monetary and non-monetary sanctions, prohibitions and mandates. For negligence and breach of contract, the optimal line is a population-level marginal cost-benefit rule weighting costs and benefits over the actors whose behaviour the line changes.
papers.ident: Theory: model of optimal threshold placement in legal rules.
papers.q: Where should legal thresholds be placed when legal treatment depends on whether an activity falls above or below a line?
papers.contribution: Characterizes the economic forces determining optimal legal thresholds and applies them to negligence due-care standards and contract breach.

papers.title: The Investment Channel of Monetary Policy: Disentangling Firm Heterogeneity

authors.inst: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

papers.q: How heterogeneous are firms' investment responses to monetary policy, and what explains that heterogeneity?
papers.summary: Most firms in most periods barely adjust investment to monetary policy; only about 5% of firm-time observations show a strong response. Most variation in sensitivity arises within firms over time, and firm observables explain only a minority of it.
papers.conclusion: The estimates provide new targets for disciplining structural models of firm heterogeneity.
papers.ident: Clustering regression of firm investment on identified monetary policy shocks, allowing latent firm-time heterogeneity.
papers.contribution: Estimates the full distribution of firm investment responses to monetary policy with a clustering regression capturing multidimensional and unobserved heterogeneity across firms and time.
papers.dataDetail: Firm-level investment panel

papers.title: Debt Sustainability and the Range of Multiple Equilibria
papers.summary: With low uncertainty the range of multiple equilibria can be large, but it shrinks as uncertainty rises and disappears when uncertainty is large enough, leaving a unique interest rate continuous in debt. Larger uncertainty weakens the effect of perceived on actual default probability.
papers.conclusion: Interpreting the source of interest rate increases in practice is difficult, which complicates central bank intervention.
papers.ident: Theory: model of sovereign debt pricing with default and uncertainty about primary balances or fiscal feedback rules.
papers.q: How large is the range of multiple equilibria in sovereign debt markets, and how does it depend on uncertainty?
papers.contribution: Characterizes the size of the multiple-equilibria region in sovereign debt markets, showing it shrinks and vanishes as uncertainty about primary balances or fiscal rules grows.

papers.title: Inference for Regression with Clustered or Spatially Correlated Data I: Framework and Clustering
papers.summary: Positive within-cluster correlation reduces the information in each observation, so unadjusted standard errors yield too-narrow intervals and over-rejecting tests. The paper sets out a general framework and details cluster-robust methods with improved finite-sample performance; a companion paper treats spatial correlation.
papers.conclusion: Such adjustments are often necessary in applied work.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: inference with within-cluster correlation and few clusters.
papers.q: How should researchers conduct inference in regressions with clustered or spatially correlated observations?
papers.contribution: Provides a general framework and practitioner guide to cluster-robust inference, emphasizing finite-sample corrections when clusters are few.

papers.title: Communicating Performance: Textual and Financial Disclosures in Private Equity
papers.summary: Early in an investment, textual discussions of portfolio companies carry substantial information about ultimate performance while interim valuations matter less; the pattern reverses over time, especially after a financing event. Results vary with both tone and content of manager disclosures.
papers.conclusion: In an opaque market, textual discussions appear to serve as a signal of general partner quality.
papers.contribution: Combines text of private equity fund reports with interim valuations to show the information content shifts from text early on to valuations later.
papers.q: How do private equity fund managers' textual and financial disclosures convey information about portfolio firm performance over the investment life?
papers.ident: Descriptive: predictive regressions of portfolio company returns on disclosure text and interim valuations.
papers.dataDetail: Private equity fund disclosures to investors and portfolio company valuations

papers.title: Reassessing the 2000s Housing Cycle After Two Decades of Research
papers.q: What caused the 2000s US housing boom and bust, according to two decades of empirical and structural research?
papers.summary: Improved fundamentals and credit expansion from automated underwriting and deregulation started the boom, followed by lower interest rates and expanding securitized and subprime credit. The persistent boom produced over-optimistic and diverging expectations; in the bust, prices overshot mainly because mortgage defaults removed buyers and contracted credit.
papers.conclusion: How these forces interact and how expectations form require further research.
papers.contribution: Synthesizes reduced-form and structural research on the 2000s housing cycle, reconciling studies by timing, place, methodology and measurement into a staged account.

papers.title: Labor Supply and Wages over the Life Cycle: Human Capital and Disability Benefits
papers.q: How do human capital, health and disability benefits interact to shape UK women's life-cycle labour supply and wages across education groups?
papers.summary: Documents three decades of UK trends in labour supply, wages, health and disability claims and how tax credit, disability and welfare reforms changed work incentives. Estimating the model on a panel of UK working-age women shows interactions between experience and health capital drive life-cycle earnings differently by education.
papers.conclusion: Interactions among disability benefit, welfare and tax-credit systems are important for understanding life-cycle hours, employment, earnings and disability claims and for policy counterfactuals.
papers.ident: Structural: dynamic life-cycle model of labour supply, human capital and disability benefit application estimated on UK women's panel data.
papers.contribution: Builds a dynamic structural life-cycle model in which human capital combines health, experience and education, adding disability benefit applications to tax and welfare incentives.
papers.dataDetail: UK panel of working-age women over three decades

papers.title: Limits to Arbitrage and Prediction Market Efficiency: the Case of PredictIt
papers.summary: Bid prices often persistently summed to more than 110, implying immediate arbitrage profits even after fees, and longshots were more overpriced than in other prediction markets. These biases were much larger than in previously studied markets during 2016-22.
papers.conclusion: Limiting stakes may undermine prediction markets' ability to accurately price event probabilities.
papers.q: Did position limits on the PredictIt political prediction market prevent arbitrage and undermine price efficiency?
papers.contribution: Documents pricing biases on PredictIt, where an $850 cap per contract limited arbitrage, showing larger inefficiencies than in earlier prediction markets.
papers.ident: Descriptive: measurement of pricing biases and arbitrage gaps on PredictIt contracts.
papers.dataDetail: PredictIt contract prices, 2016-2022

papers.title: Latent Human Capital: How Early Investments in Parents Buffer Against Future Schooling Shocks
papers.q: Do early investments in parenting generate latent human capital that protects children when school inputs are later disrupted?
papers.summary: Before the closures, treatment effects on achievement had faded to zero in all groups. During Covid-19 closures, test scores fell by roughly 0.25-0.30 SD in control and preschool groups but only 0.11 SD in the parenting group (difference p = 0.01).
papers.ident: Random assignment to a parenting program, preschool or control at ages 3-5, combined with Covid-19 school closures a decade later.
papers.contribution: Combines an early-childhood field experiment with Covid-19 school closures ten years later to reveal effects of a parenting program that had faded out.
papers.conclusion: Parenting programs can create latent human capital visible only when school inputs fail, so standard evaluations of early childhood programs may miss state-contingent value.
papers.dataDetail: Long-run follow-up of an early-childhood field experiment with children's test scores

papers.title: Physicians' Occupational Licensing and the Quantity-Quality Trade-off
papers.q: How does physician occupational licensing trade off the quantity and quality of doctors in public hospitals in Chile?
papers.summary: More physicians improve patient outcomes in public hospitals, while lower-quality physicians, measured by licensing exam performance, worsen them. A theoretical framework incorporating these estimates evaluates locally changing licensing stringency.
papers.ident: Quasi-exogenous variation in physician supply from immigration to Chile and domestic medical school growth, fed into a theoretical framework.
papers.contribution: Quantifies the licensing quantity-quality trade-off using an unprecedented physician immigration wave to Chile and domestic medical school growth.
papers.dataDetail: Chilean public hospital patient outcomes and physician licensing exam scores

papers.title: Estimating Heterogeneous Impacts with Endogenous Participation and Non-Compliance

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.q: How can heterogeneous RCT impacts be estimated when the subgroup status is endogenous and unobserved in the control group?
papers.summary: Applied to a clustered RCT of an early-years intervention in Ghana, the method separates impacts on households participating actively from those participating only passively. For some outcomes, properly estimated heterogeneous impacts differ substantially from a naive estimator.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: identification of heterogeneous effects with endogenous, partly unobserved participation status in RCTs.
papers.contribution: Develops an approach using treatment-sample information and a noisy signal of status to identify heterogeneous impacts under minimal assumptions.
papers.dataDetail: Clustered RCT data on an early-years intervention in Ghana

papers.title: The Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Pollution on Health
papers.summary: Linking personnel records of roughly 150,000 U.S. Army soldiers to annual PM2.5 measures, sustained exposure substantially increases circulatory disease, particularly hypertension, with mixed and specification-sensitive evidence on respiratory conditions. Shorter exposure has little detectable effect, consistent with a cumulative health burden.
papers.ident: IV using quasi-random initial duty-station assignments as instrument for career-average annual PM2.5 exposure.
papers.contribution: Provides the first causal evidence on long-term PM2.5 exposure at contemporary ambient levels and chronic disease, using quasi-random Army duty-station assignments as an instrument.
papers.q: Does long-term exposure to fine particulate matter cause chronic disease among young, initially healthy U.S. Army soldiers?
papers.conclusion: Even moderate long-term air pollution can erode health capital in ways that studies of short-run variation miss.
