papers.dataDetail: Personnel records of about 150,000 U.S. Army soldiers linked to high-resolution annual PM2.5 measures.

papers.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation
papers.q: Which workers left the labor force after the COVID recession, and what explains their exit?
papers.summary: Labor force exit is persistent, especially among low-income and low-skill workers, with low-skilled unmarried men by far the most likely to exit. School closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments and unemployment benefits explain little, and neither does occupational or firm-quality upgrading. Leavers do not on average make up the lost income; self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of lost W-2 income.
papers.conclusion: The facts suggest that willingness to work for low pay fell and preferences for leisure and job flexibility rose, with implications for tax policy, fiscal projections and labor market dynamics.
papers.contribution: Assembles a tax-data panel with newly added worker occupation information to document persistent post-COVID labor force exit by occupation, income and skill.
papers.ident: Descriptive: panel of tax records with occupation information, tracking labor force exit by worker group after COVID.
papers.dataDetail: Panel of tax data with newly assembled worker occupation information.

papers.title: The Geopolitical Trap: How Great Power Rivalry Protects Rising Powers
papers.summary: Studies, as the title indicates, how great power rivalry protects rising powers.

papers.title: Inference for Regression with Clustered or Spatially Correlated Data II: Spatial Correlation
papers.summary: Failing to adjust standard errors for spatial correlation gives confidence intervals that are too narrow and tests that over-reject. When correlation dampens with distance the standard method is Conley's spatial HAC, which works poorly when spatial persistence is high, so alternatives are needed; regressions should also control for spatial trends to avoid spurious correlation.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: standard-error inference under spatial correlation.
papers.q: How should inference be conducted for regressions with spatially correlated data when spatial correlation declines with distance?
papers.contribution: Reviews inference methods for regressions with spatially correlated data, including Conley's spatial HAC and the alternatives needed when spatial persistence is high.

papers.title: High and Rising Institutional Concentration of Award-Winning Economists
papers.q: How has the institutional concentration of award-winning researchers evolved across 18 fields, and why is economics becoming more concentrated?
papers.summary: Concentration of prizewinners' affiliations declined in all fields except economics, shifting from a few science-strong universities in high-income countries to more diverse institutions worldwide. Prizewinning economists have become more concentrated, making economics the most concentrated field, which the paper associates with stronger sorting by institutional prestige, lower reliance on specialized equipment, and assessing findings by synthesis of evidence rather than decisive experiments or proofs.
papers.conclusion: The paper discusses the benefits and costs of the high and rising institutional concentration of prizewinning economists.
papers.contribution: Assembles affiliations of nearly 6,000 award-winning researchers in 18 fields since the 1820s to compare institutional concentration across disciplines, singling out economics.
papers.ident: Descriptive: concentration of award winners' institutional affiliations across 18 fields, focusing on the 1960s onward.
papers.dataDetail: Affiliations of nearly 6,000 award-winning researchers in 18 fields, 1820s-2020s.

papers.title: Keeping up with the Joneses: FDI, supply chain linkages, and industrial emissions

authors.inst: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

papers.summary: Studies how foreign direct investment and supply chain linkages relate to industrial emissions, as the title indicates.

papers.title: The Effect of School Closures during the Pandemic on Parental Labor Supply in China
papers.summary: Studies the effect of pandemic school closures on parental labor supply in China, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Supply shocks and inflation: Timely insights from financial markets
papers.summary: Examines how financial market data can provide timely information on supply shocks and inflation, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Emissions abatement under a rate-based emissions trading system: facility-level evidence from China
papers.summary: Provides facility-level evidence from China on emissions abatement under a rate-based emissions trading system, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class
papers.summary: Exposure in childhood neighbourhoods increases marriage between high- and low-parent-income groups but has no detectable effect on White-Black marriage. A spatial marriage model attributes more than one third of marital sorting by class to residential segregation, against less than 5 percent of sorting by race.
papers.ident: IV using whether other race and class groups had more similar-age, opposite-sex children in childhood neighbourhoods; spatial marriage model
papers.q: Does childhood exposure to other race and class groups raise intergroup marriage in the United States?
papers.contribution: Instruments exposure with whether other race and class groups had more similar-age, opposite-sex children in childhood neighbourhoods, and quantifies residential segregation's role in marital sorting.

papers.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty
papers.q: Do retrieval failures cause Zambian farmers to underestimate upcoming spending and undersave, and does prompting recall improve consumption smoothing?
papers.summary: Zambian farmers underestimate upcoming spending by 50%. Treated individuals increase remembered expenses by 36%-60%, hold 15% higher savings six weeks later, enter the hungry season with one additional month of savings, and have 9% higher crop revenue the next year through additional farm investment.
papers.contribution: Documents retrieval failures in expense forecasting and tests a randomized recall-prompting intervention that provides no external information, tracing effects through savings, investment and crop revenue.
papers.ident: RCT randomizing a prompt to think through future expenses associatively in categories, among Zambian farmers; replicated on beliefs among low-income Americans.
papers.dataDetail: Field experiment with Zambian farmers; belief replication among low-income Americans.

papers.title: Truth Elicitation in a Nonstrategic Environment
papers.summary: A principal awards a prize by giving each party a text describing when it deserves it and asking both to report the state; parties cheat through known procedures. Implementation holds when, after any disagreement, the truthful party is the only one who could not have produced its story had the rival's been true.
papers.q: How can a principal tell which of two nonstrategic parties is truthful when each cheats through a known procedure?
papers.contribution: Develops a one-way cheating principle under which the texts given to the parties make the liar identifiable whenever their reports disagree.
papers.ident: Theory: mechanism design with nonstrategic parties who follow known cheating procedures

papers.title: The long-term effects of teachers’ gender stereotypes on labor outcomes
papers.summary: Studies the long-term effects of teachers' gender stereotypes on labor outcomes, as the title indicates.

papers.title: In sickness and in health: Motivating improved healthcare using holistic patient contracts
papers.summary: Studies how holistic patient contracts can motivate improved healthcare, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Disparate Treatment of the Irish in 19th Century English Courtrooms

authors.inst: London School of Economics and Political Science

papers.summary: Studies disparate treatment of the Irish in 19th century English courtrooms, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Nonparametric identification of first-price auction with unobserved competition: A density discontinuity framework
papers.summary: In independent private value first-price auctions where only winning bids are observed, bidders observing N produce discontinuities in the winning bid density that identify the distribution of N. This extends, under testable conditions, to N as potential buyers who bid with unknown probability, and to additive unobserved heterogeneity from parametric distributions.
papers.q: Can the distribution of bidders and private values in first-price auctions be nonparametrically identified from winning bids alone?
papers.contribution: Shows that discontinuities in the winning bid density identify the distribution of the number of bidders, enabling second-step identification of the private value distribution.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: nonparametric identification of first-price auctions from winning bids using density discontinuities.

papers.title: Oil Prices, Monetary Policy, and Inflation Surges
papers.q: How did oil price shocks and monetary policy accommodation contribute to the recent surge and fall in inflation?
papers.summary: The estimated framework shows that both oil shocks and shocks to policy accommodation played important roles in the rise of inflation.
papers.contribution: Develops a simple quantitative New Keynesian model disciplined by identified oil and monetary shocks, then recovers shocks without targeting inflation.
papers.ident: Quantitative: New Keynesian model estimated using identified oil price shocks and monetary shocks.

papers.title: Labor Market Discrimination and the Racial Unemployment Gap: Can Monetary Policy Make a Difference?
papers.q: Can employer discrimination explain the racial unemployment gap, and can monetary policy reduce it?
papers.summary: The model explains why Black workers experience higher, more volatile unemployment than White workers, a disparity unexplained by observables. A rule responding to employment shortfalls from its maximum level raises inflation and does not reduce the racial unemployment gap, and a rule responding to the gap itself also fails to reduce it.
papers.ident: Quantitative: New Keynesian model with search frictions, endogenous separations and employer discrimination used for monetary policy counterfactuals.
papers.contribution: Builds a New Keynesian model with frictional labor markets, endogenous separations and employer discrimination to explain Black-White unemployment gaps and assess monetary policy rules by race.

papers.title: Wage Adjustment in Efficient Long-Term Employment Relationships
papers.summary: The model yields new insights into the distribution of pay changes among job stayers, a near-memorylessness property whereby hiring wages have limited influence on later wages and allocation, and a crucial role for recruitment and retention bonuses in sustaining efficient relationships.
papers.contribution: Presents an analytically solvable model of efficient long-term employment relationships with sporadic wage adjustment due to renegotiation costs.
papers.q: How do efficient long-term employment relationships adjust wages given productivity shocks, outside offers and renegotiation costs?
papers.ident: Theory: analytically solvable model of long-term employment with renegotiation costs, productivity shocks and outside offers.

papers.title: Optimal Taxation of Inflation
papers.q: Can a tax on inflation, levied on firms in proportion to their price or wage increases, stabilize inflation?
papers.summary: TIP effectively corrects externalities in pricing decisions, tackles excessive inflation and reduces output volatility. It addresses cost-push shocks while monetary policy addresses demand shocks, and unlike price controls it does not exacerbate relative price distortions.
papers.contribution: Analyzes a tax on inflation policy (TIP) and shows it corrects externalities in firms' pricing decisions and complements monetary policy rather than substituting for it.
papers.ident: Theory: New Keynesian pricing model with a tax proportional to firms' price or wage increases.

papers.title: Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.summary: Humanity is likely below replacement fertility as of 2026, with the fall concentrated in low- and middle-income countries and among poorer, less educated women. The common component peaked in 1978; country-specific trends drive fertility down today, 219 of them negative and none leveling off, and commonly cited mechanisms cannot account for the pattern.
papers.conclusion: Nothing in an economy pushes fertility back to 2.1, with slow growth as a main economic consequence.
papers.q: Why is fertility falling below replacement across low- and middle-income countries, and what are the economic consequences?
papers.contribution: Fits a single-factor model to 236 countries since 1950 to separate common from country-specific fertility trends, and conjectures that modernity itself drives the decline.
papers.ident: Descriptive: single-factor model of country fertility trends, decomposing common and country-specific components.
papers.dataDetail: Fertility data for 236 countries since 1950.

papers.title: Do Workfare Programs Live Up to Their Promises? Experimental Evidence from Côte d'Ivoire

authors.inst: Centre de Recherche en Économie et Statistique

papers.q: What are the contemporaneous and post-program effects of a public works program for urban youth in Côte d'Ivoire?
papers.summary: During the program, employment rises only slightly but there is a shift toward wage jobs, with higher earnings, savings, work habits and well-being. After the program there is no lasting impact on employment or behaviors, with only limited earnings gains from independent activities.
papers.contribution: Evaluates a randomized public works program offering seven months of minimum-wage employment with training, tracking effects during and after the program and using machine learning to study targeting.
papers.conclusion: Machine learning heterogeneity analysis shows that alternative targeting approaches can substantially improve welfare.
papers.ident: RCT of a public works program with entrepreneurship or job search training for urban youth; machine learning for heterogeneity.

papers.title: Innovation through Inventor Mobility: Evidence from Noncompete Agreements
papers.summary: Stronger enforceability has a significant negative effect on innovation, even larger for the most novel and innovative patents and firms. The effects cannot be explained by entry alone and likely result from reduced knowledge flows.
papers.contribution: Leverages plausibly exogenous state-level changes in the enforceability of noncompete agreements to estimate the causal effect on innovation.
papers.q: Do stricter state enforcement of noncompete agreements reduce innovation?
papers.conclusion: Labor mobility plays a crucial role in spreading knowledge across firms.
papers.ident: Difference-in-differences exploiting state-level changes in noncompete enforceability.

papers.title: An LLM Workflow That Reproduces, Improves, and Extends Published Economics Research
papers.summary: The workflow flags discrepancies in 3,460 articles or their appendices, reduces a calculation's computation time by more than a factor of 10 at similar or greater accuracy in 496 articles, and develops an extension aligned with the original goals and assumptions in 923 articles.
papers.q: Can an LLM workflow reproduce, improve and extend published economics articles from their replication packages?
papers.contribution: Introduces an open-source LLM workflow that reproduces results, flags discrepancies, speeds up calculations and develops extensions, applied to 4,452 replication packages from five economics journals.
papers.ident: Descriptive: automated LLM reproduction, sensitivity analysis and extension of published replication packages.
papers.dataDetail: 4,452 replication packages from five economics journals.

papers.title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Remote Work’s Impact on Employment in the UK
papers.q: Does the rise of remote work increase employment among disabled and older workers in the UK?
papers.summary: Rising work from home increases employment of disabled and older workers in the UK. It also decreases commute time and wages for both groups, with no effect on hours worked.
papers.ident: Compares occupations with high versus low growth in work from home during the pandemic, instrumented with pre-pandemic remote work scores.
papers.contribution: Tests the employment effects of remote work for disabled and older UK workers, using the pandemic's rise in work from home as a quasi-experiment instrumented with pre-pandemic remote work scores.

papers.title: The Early Impacts of AI on Employment among Recent College Graduates
papers.q: Did AI raise unemployment among recent college graduates in summer 2026?
papers.summary: Unemployment rates did not spike in summer 2026 relative to previous summers and did not rise significantly relative to older college graduates or young workers without a degree. The expanded definition including those who report wanting a job adds nearly two percentage points to recent graduates' unemployment rate.
papers.contribution: Provides the first CPS-based estimates of AI effects on recent graduates' unemployment in summer 2026, and analyzes an expanded unemployment definition including those who want a job.
papers.ident: Compares recent college graduates' summer 2026 unemployment with prior summers and with older graduates and non-graduates, with agnostic treatment timing.
papers.dataDetail: CPS microdata, including June-August 2026.

papers.title: Optimal progressive pension systems and heterogeneous labor market risk
papers.q: How should optimal pension systems account for heterogeneous employment stability and labor market risk?
papers.summary: The optimal pension system is substantially more progressive than current Social Security, with a benefit schedule approaching a floor, and abolishing the Social Security cap raises progressivity further; together these generate welfare gains of 0.94% of lifetime consumption for new entrants. Insurance gains dominate the distortions to human capital investment and labor supply.
papers.ident: Quantitative: life-cycle model with heterogeneous job-separation risk and endogenous human capital, calibrated to the U.S. economy.
papers.contribution: Develops a life-cycle model with heterogeneous job-separation risk, endogenous human capital, saving and retirement in a frictional labor market, calibrated to the U.S., to design pension progressivity.

papers.title: The Great Accretion and the Great Depression
papers.q: Could over-investment driven by process and product innovation have helped trigger the Great Depression?
papers.summary: Proof-of-concept simulations assess whether excitement about technology, slowing new product development and satiated demand, and continuous process innovation, can help explain the Great Depression. The paper's answer is yes.
papers.contribution: Proposes a macroeconomic model incorporating both process and product innovation to explore whether over-accumulation of investment in the 1920s contributed to the Great Depression.
papers.ident: Quantitative: macroeconomic model with process and product innovation, simulated in proof-of-concept exercises.

papers.title: Accounting for Cross-Country Income Differences Revisited
papers.summary: Advances in measuring inputs, mostly human capital, raise the estimated contribution of inputs: the preferred estimate is that inputs account for 55-70 percent of GDP per worker differences, versus 30 percent under the classic specification. Progress also includes measuring factors such as management quality previously bundled into TFP.
papers.contribution: Reviews two decades of advances in measuring labor, physical and human capital inputs and moving beyond Cobb-Douglas production functions in development accounting.
papers.q: How has development accounting evolved since Caselli (2005), and how much of cross-country income differences do inputs explain?
papers.conclusion: The review highlights new implications of these advances, areas for future research, and the limitations of development accounting.
papers.ident: Descriptive: review of development accounting decompositions of cross-country income differences.

papers.title: Detection of Collusive Networks in Multistage Auctions
papers.q: How can cartels be detected in multistage auctions where bidders revise initial bids downward?
papers.summary: Because initial bids are shaded, close initial bids indicate similar costs and a strong incentive to undercut rivals. The algorithm predicts sanctions by Ukraine's Antimonopoly Committee: classified pairs are nine times more likely to be sanctioned.
papers.contribution: Develops a method that classifies firm pairs as collusive if they fail to update bids against each other relative to pairs with similarly close initial bids, allowing collusion only among cartel members.
papers.ident: Descriptive/structural: pair-level screen comparing bid updating among firm pairs with close initial bids in multistage auctions.
papers.dataDetail: Ukrainian multistage procurement auctions and Antimonopoly Committee sanctions.

papers.title: Early Grade Retention Harms Adult Earnings
papers.summary: Third-grade retention reduces annual earnings at age 26 by $3,477 (19 percent). It temporarily improves test scores but increases absenteeism, violent behavior and juvenile crime, and reduces high school graduation; effects on community college and public university enrollment are not statistically significant.
papers.ident: Fuzzy regression discontinuity around the Texas third-grade reading test retention threshold.
papers.contribution: Provides new causal evidence on early grade retention using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design on Texas's reading test-based retention policy.
papers.q: How does third-grade retention under Texas's reading test-based policy affect educational, behavioral and labor market outcomes?
papers.dataDetail: Texas administrative education and earnings data.

papers.title: Deep Learning as a Projection Method for Solving Economic Models
papers.summary: Reframing deep learning as projection suggests a single toolkit with varied approximation methods, residual criteria and evaluation designs. In low and moderate dimensions, linear-basis and sparse-grid methods are often more accurate, faster and easier to verify, while in high dimensions an appropriate function space can avoid the curse of dimensionality.
papers.contribution: Argues that neural-network solvers are least-squares projection methods with adaptive nonlinear parameterization, placing deep learning inside the projection family.
papers.q: Is deep learning a new paradigm for solving dynamic economic models, or a form of classical projection method?
papers.ident: Econometric theory: classification of neural-network solvers as projection methods for dynamic economic models.

papers.title: Early Results from the RESET Demonstration Project: Inflation in Food at Home
papers.summary: The paper evaluates the new measures against current official statistics and as novel measures capturing consumer choice dynamics more accurately, discusses challenges in producing credible official statistics from transactions data, and reports recent Food at Home inflation trends.
papers.conclusion: The project points toward official economic statistics rebuilt on modern transactions data and technology.
papers.contribution: Introduces new Food at Home inflation measures built from item-level transactions data in the RESET Demonstration Project, and compares them to official statistics.
papers.q: Can item-level transactions data produce better inflation measures for Food at Home than current official statistics?
papers.ident: Descriptive: price and sales indices constructed from item-level transactions data and compared with official inflation statistics.
papers.dataDetail: Item-level transactions data on food at home.

papers.title: Together or apart? Migration, education access, and intergenerational mobility in China

authors.inst: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics

papers.summary: Studies how migration, education access and intergenerational mobility relate in China, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Deadwood Labor? The Effects of Eliminating Employment Protection for Older Workers
papers.q: What are the effects of eliminating employment protection for older workers at Sweden's mandatory retirement age of 67?
papers.summary: Employment falls by about 10 percent and average earnings by about 20 percent at age 67; 8 percent of jobs separate immediately, mainly those with stronger initial protection (long tenure, last-in-first-out firms) and in the public sector. Wages appear rigid, but hours reductions produce an 8 percent drop in earnings conditional on staying in the job.
papers.contribution: Analyzes Sweden's mandatory retirement at 67 as the removal of employment protection, uncovering sizable intensive-margin hours reductions in continuing jobs.
papers.ident: Discontinuity in employment protection at the mandatory retirement age of 67 in Sweden.

papers.title: Optimal Population Growth in the Diamond OLG Model
papers.q: What population growth rate maximizes steady-state welfare in the Diamond OLG model?
papers.summary: Lower population growth raises output per worker but reduces the worker-to-retiree ratio. The optimal growth rate may be negative, so shrinking populations can be optimal, and a pay-as-you-go social security system lowers the optimal growth rate.
papers.contribution: Shows that, under mild parameter restrictions, an optimal population growth rate exists in an OLG model that trades off output per worker against the ratio of workers to retirees.
papers.ident: Theory: steady-state welfare in a Diamond overlapping-generations model with population growth and pay-as-you-go social security.

papers.title: The Dynamics of Development in a Zero-Sum World
papers.q: How do zero-sum environments and demotivating beliefs affect cultural change, innovation and long-term growth?
papers.summary: Demotivating beliefs limit excessive competition in zero-sum environments but suppress effort, reducing learning-by-doing and production spillovers, thereby inhibiting innovation as a cultural evolutionary kludge. The model is applied to the cultural changes associated with Western Europe's rise after 1500.
papers.contribution: Introduces innovation into a framework in which zero-sum environments generate demotivating beliefs, showing they can improve static efficiency while impeding long-term growth.
papers.ident: Theory: model of cultural evolution with zero-sum environments, demotivating beliefs and innovation.

papers.title: Injury, Workload, and the Strategic Response of Coaches in the NBA
papers.q: Does workload causally raise injury risk in the NBA, and do coaches act on private information about injury risk?
papers.summary: Work causally raises injury risk, contrasting with the spurious negative correlation commonly found in sports medicine studies. Coaches rest players in response to injury risk shocks, and by acting on this private information they can raise player productivity.
papers.contribution: Instruments workload with teammate absence to estimate its causal effect on injury and shows that coaches rest players in response to injury risk shocks.
papers.ident: IV using teammate absence as instrument for player workload.
papers.dataDetail: NBA player-game data.

papers.title: Treatment evaluation at the intensive and extensive margins
papers.summary: A large share of selection-indifferent units, for example from non-compliance, makes the bounds irregular, so conventional asymptotic inference for Lee bounds can mislead; smoothed outer identification regions solve this. The semiparametrically efficient estimators accommodate high-dimensional covariates, and an application to active labor market policy shows the indifference population is empirically prevalent while supporting earlier results under weaker assumptions.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: sharp bounds for treatment effects under selection at intensive and extensive margins, with debiased ML estimation.
papers.contribution: Provides sharp bounds for average treatment effects under conditional monotonicity for all principal strata, with smoothed inference and debiased machine learning estimators.
papers.q: How can treatment effects be bounded in selective samples without instruments or parametric assumptions, including when many units' selection is indifferent to treatment?
papers.dataDetail: Active labor market policy evaluation data.

papers.title: Do Water Audits Work?
papers.summary: Financial incentives substantially raise audit take-up and, among compliers, cut water use by about 17 per cent over two months; incentive size matters for participation but not conservation. Effects become undetectable after roughly two months, so net welfare gains are typically below £1 per capita, and targeting high-use households doubles short-run effects but not welfare.
papers.ident: Natural field experiment randomly assigning about 45,000 UK households to behavioural encouragements to complete an online home water audit.
papers.q: Do residential water audits, with financial incentives to complete them, cause lasting water conservation and welfare gains?
papers.contribution: Provides causal evidence from a natural field experiment in the UK randomly assigning about 45,000 households to different behavioural encouragements to complete an online water audit.
papers.conclusion: Audits and incentives induce meaningful short-run conservation, but policy value depends critically on whether conservation persists.
papers.dataDetail: About 45,000 UK households; water consumption data.

papers.title: Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the Metco Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
papers.summary: Attending a suburban school raises math and English scores, reduces dropout and increases on-time high school graduation, and raises four-year college aspirations, enrollment, graduation and adult earnings. Effects are largest for students whose parents did not attend college and for boys, and participants are more likely to be tracked into lower-performing classes.
papers.ident: 2SLS comparing applicants with and without enrollment offers, exploiting waitlist assignment priorities.
papers.q: What are the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school through Boston's METCO voluntary desegregation program on urban students of color?
papers.contribution: Estimates METCO effects using 2SLS with waitlist assignment priorities, linking birth records, application data and later outcomes including adult earnings.
papers.dataDetail: METCO application data linked to birth records, school records and earnings.

papers.title: Panel data models with interactive fixed effects and (relatively) small T
papers.q: Can the least squares estimator of panel models with interactive fixed effects be made consistent when T is small?
papers.summary: The properties carry over to large n, large T provided T/n tends to zero. This contrasts with the usual case, where least squares is generally inconsistent with n large and T fixed and asymptotically biased when both are large.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: transformed least squares estimation of linear panel models with interactive fixed effects and small T.
papers.contribution: Introduces a transformation that renders Bai's (2009) least squares estimator consistent and asymptotically unbiased with n large and T fixed, termed the transformed least squares estimator.

papers.title: Recommendation Design: Can Mediators Implement Correlated Equilibria?
papers.q: Can individuals act as mediators who design incentive-compatible recommendation devices that implement correlated equilibria?
papers.summary: Most participants successfully implement correlated equilibria across games, especially where coordination yields benefits. Across objectives, many participants initially favor fair and efficient devices even when these properties are not incentivized.
papers.contribution: Reports a novel experiment in which participants design recommendation devices for rational robot agents across games and mediator objectives.
papers.conclusion: Fairness and efficiency serve as important heuristics in recommendation design.
papers.ident: Lab experiment varying the games played by robot agents and the mediator's objective.
papers.dataDetail: Laboratory experiment with human mediators and robot agents.

papers.title: Mobile internet connectivity and household wealth in the Philippines
papers.q: Does mobile internet connectivity increase household wealth in the Philippines?
papers.summary: Mobile internet connectivity increases household wealth, across education levels and most strongly in urban areas. Mechanisms include stimulated activity in key sectors, better educational outcomes and increased female labor force participation, mainly in occasional work; an event study suggests tower rollout may facilitate international labor migration and remittances.
papers.ident: IV using proximity to submarine cable landing points for local mobile connectivity; event study of tower rollout on migration and remittances.
papers.contribution: Measures local connectivity using geocoded cell towers and identifies causal effects with an instrument based on proximity to submarine cable landing points.
papers.dataDetail: Geocoded cell tower data and household survey data from the Philippines.

papers.title: Information access and college admission outcomes

authors.inst: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

papers.summary: Studies how access to information affects college admission outcomes, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Propagation of Immigration Shocks through Firm-to-Firm Trade Networks

authors.inst: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey

papers.q: How does an immigration shock to a region propagate through firm-to-firm supply chains across Turkey?
papers.summary: Firms with pre-existing upstream or downstream links to refugee-hosting regions show positive spillovers, and the shock expands interprovincial trade and forms new firm-to-firm linkages. Standard spatial approaches comparing regions by migration rates conflate propagation with direct effects, overstating direct effects on sales and employment and masking a negative direct wage effect at the firm level.
papers.contribution: Uses the unexpected arrival of Syrian refugees in Turkish border regions to estimate spillovers through supply chains on firms' sales, employment and wages, and on interprovincial trade networks.
papers.ident: Exposure to Syrian refugee arrival via pre-existing firm-to-firm trade links to border refugee-hosting regions in Turkey.
papers.dataDetail: Turkish firm-to-firm trade network, sales, employment and wage data.

papers.title: Out with the new, in with the old? Supranational bank supervision and the composition of firm investment

authors.inst: Center for Economic Research and Graduate Education – Economics Institute

papers.summary: Studies how supranational bank supervision relates to the composition of firm investment, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Robust estimation and inference for high-dimensional panel data models

authors.inst: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

papers.q: How can robust estimation and inference be conducted in high-dimensional panel data models with correlated, heteroskedastic errors?
papers.summary: The framework allows non-Gaussian, serially and cross-sectionally correlated and heteroskedastic errors and a thresholded long-run covariance matrix estimator. Its usefulness is shown for a high-dimensional panel with interactive effects, with extensive simulated and real data examples.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: LASSO-based estimation and inference with a thresholded HAC estimator in high-dimensional panels.
papers.contribution: Provides a toolkit with Nagaev-type concentration inequalities, a non-asymptotic LASSO bound, node-wise LASSO asymptotic normality, and a thresholded HAC estimator allowing the number of regressors to exceed the sample size.

papers.title: Inattention, Information Provision, and (Failures of) Revealed Preference
papers.summary: Baseline attention is systematically distorted, and information about a desirable attribute, even when known, redundant and randomly assigned, greatly increases attention to it and distracts from others while raising average demand. Information experiments with passive controls can mislead and even give the wrong sign: reducing overoptimism about an attribute boosts demand for its good.
papers.ident: Induced-preference experiment with randomized redundant information; theory of inattention in demand estimation.
papers.q: Does differential inattention bias preference estimates from information experiments with passive control groups?
papers.contribution: Shows in a multi-attribute induced-preference experiment that information provision shifts attention across attributes, biasing standard revealed-preference estimates, and that active control groups correct the sign.
papers.conclusion: Active control-group experiments yield preference estimates with the correct sign, theoretically and experimentally.
papers.dataDetail: Multi-attribute induced-preference experiment.

papers.title: Banks and informality: Two perspectives of microenterprises’ balance sheets

authors.inst: Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies

papers.summary: Studies banks and informality through two perspectives of microenterprises' balance sheets, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Motivating job seekers. A field experiment
papers.summary: Reports a field experiment on motivating job seekers, as the title indicates.

papers.title: The cost of job loss in carbon-intensive sectors: Evidence from Germany

authors.inst: Organisation de Coopération et de Développement Economiques
Organisation de Coopération et de Développement Economiques
Organisation de Coopération et de Développement Economiques

papers.summary: Studies the cost of job loss in carbon-intensive sectors in Germany, as the title indicates.

papers.title: Real-time monitoring for stock return predictability in nonstationary volatility environments
papers.q: How can episodic stock return predictability be detected in real time when volatility is nonstationary?
papers.summary: Monitoring entails repeated application of end-of-sample predictability statistics and so requires accounting for multiple testing, unknown regressor persistence and predictive regression endogeneity. Nonparametric adjustments handle time-varying volatility without assuming a volatility model, which otherwise can cause spurious detection of predictability.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: sequential CUSUM-type monitoring of predictive regressions under nonstationary volatility.
papers.contribution: Proposes real-time monitoring procedures, preferably a CUSUM-type procedure based on a predictive-power moment condition, robust to persistence, endogeneity, multiple testing and time-varying volatility.

papers.title: Early results from the RESET demonstration project: Inflation in food at home
papers.summary: The paper evaluates the new measures against current official statistics and as novel measures capturing consumer choice dynamics more accurately, discusses challenges in producing credible official statistics from transactions data, and reports recent Food at Home inflation trends.
papers.contribution: Introduces new Food at Home inflation measures built from item-level transactions data in the RESET Demonstration Project, and compares them to official statistics.
papers.q: Can item-level transactions data produce better inflation measures for Food at Home than current official statistics?
papers.conclusion: The project points toward official economic statistics rebuilt on modern transactions data and technology.
papers.ident: Descriptive: price and sales indices constructed from item-level transactions data and compared with official inflation statistics.
papers.dataDetail: Item-level transactions data on food at home.

papers.title: Jackknife variance estimators for two-way clustering with serially correlated time effects
papers.summary: Proposes jackknife variance estimators for two-way clustering with serially correlated time effects, as the title indicates.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: jackknife variance estimation under two-way clustering with serially correlated time effects.

papers.title: Decolonization, legitimacy and fiscal capacity: Event study evidence from Africa
papers.summary: There are no discernible pre-trends and fiscal capacity rises substantially starting about 5-6 years after decolonization, robust to alternative explanations, alternative control groups and generalized synthetic control. The effect is not explained by democratization or improved public goods provision.
papers.ident: Staggered DiD implemented as a stacked event study around decolonization dates across African countries, with generalized synthetic control.
papers.contribution: Uses a new dataset on African fiscal history from 1900 to 2015 and a stacked event study to estimate the effect of decolonization on revenue from hard-to-collect taxes.
papers.q: How did decolonization affect fiscal capacity in Africa?
papers.conclusion: The authors' framework posits that postcolonial states' higher legitimacy improved citizens' tax morale, enabling more revenue from hard-to-collect sources.
papers.dataDetail: Fiscal history dataset for African countries, 1900-2015.

papers.title: Incentivizing Self-Protection From Wildfires
papers.summary: Incentives of $100 to $500 led up to 12% of homeowners to schedule free assessments, versus at most 3% under information-only approaches. Responses are largest for owners of more valuable homes, baseline wildfire risk does not predict responsiveness, and vegetation measures give noisy estimates of effects on endline vegetation.
papers.ident: Two randomized field experiments offering $100-$500 incentives to Oregon homeowners to schedule defensible space assessments.
papers.q: Do financial incentives induce homeowners to take up wildfire defensible space assessments more than information alone?
papers.contribution: Reports two randomized field experiments incentivizing thousands of Oregon homeowners to participate in fire department programs, and links behavioral elasticities to pricing of wildfire risk in insurance.
papers.dataDetail: Randomized experiments with thousands of Oregon homeowners; vegetation measures on the ground and remotely sensed.

papers.title: Knowledge diffusion, rising inequality, and the dynamics of a pulled front
papers.summary: In the model, individual income shocks are Brownian noise with near-zero drift, and growth comes from occasional frontier advances that create learning opportunities for others. Long-run growth rises with both shock variance and the diffusion rate, and the calibrated model closely reproduces the U.S. wage distribution from 1991 to 2023.
papers.ident: Quantitative: knowledge-diffusion growth model calibrated to U.S. wage micro data, 1991-2023.
papers.contribution: Develops a growth model in which workers raise income by learning from higher-paid workers, so growth is a pulled front driven by random advances at the frontier.
papers.q: How do learning from higher-paid workers and random income shocks generate growth and the evolving U.S. wage distribution?
papers.dataDetail: U.S. wage micro data, 1991-2023.

papers.title: Well-Being Salience in Corporate Disclosures and Worker Health
papers.q: How does a firm's orientation toward employee well-being, as expressed in its public disclosures, shape its workers' health and sickness absence?
papers.summary: Using worker mobility between Danish firms in 2013-2022, workers moving to higher-salience firms take substantially more sickness absence, while their health care use does not change. This pattern points to a behavioral change rather than worsening health.
papers.conclusion: Firms shape how workers act on their health, and the language of routine disclosures reveals workplace features that administrative data miss.
papers.contribution: Constructs a firm-level well-being salience score from corporate disclosures with language models and links it to population-wide Danish health and absence registers.
papers.ident: Event-study of worker moves between firms with different well-being salience scores, 2013-2022.
papers.dataDetail: Danish population-wide health and sickness absence registers linked to firm disclosures, 2013-2022.

papers.title: Governing Global Externalities: Investor Voice Amid Fragmented Policy
papers.q: Can investor voice address global externalities from a multinational firm when regulation is fragmented across jurisdictions?
papers.summary: In the model both channels can reduce externalities, but their relative effectiveness depends on political frictions abroad. When frictions block foreign regulation, leakage weakens advocacy and strengthens stewardship; when foreign regulation is feasible, stewardship can crowd out it while local advocacy can crowd it in.
papers.contribution: Models and compares two investor channels, corporate stewardship and policy advocacy, under political frictions and leakage across jurisdictions.
papers.ident: Theory: model of a multinational firm, regulators and investors with regulatory arbitrage and leakage.

papers.title: Responses to Extreme Price Changes: Evidence from the Residential Demand for Natural Gas
papers.q: How did Georgian households' residential gas consumption respond to an extreme price change during the pandemic lockdown?
papers.summary: Gas was effectively free up to a monthly consumption allowance from November 2020 to February 2021. Controlling for weather, the policy raised consumption by 2-7% in treated households relative to controls, implying a price elasticity of demand of about -6.5% to -11%.
papers.ident: DiD comparing households with free gas only during the pandemic to pipeline-area residents with free gas every winter, controlling for weather.
papers.contribution: Exploits Georgia's free-gas policy of 2020-2021, with a control group of permanent residents who receive free gas every winter, to estimate responses to a near-zero price.
papers.dataDetail: Residential gas consumption of households in the Republic of Georgia, winter 2020-2021.

papers.title: Expectations and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
papers.q: How do subjective expectations and risk premia drive the sensitivity of long-term yields to short-term interest rates?
papers.summary: For short and medium maturities, the sensitivity of long-term yields to the short rate is driven mainly by expectations rather than risk premia. Expectations of long-term yields respond with systematic wedges relative to expectations of shorter-maturity yields, reflecting structural inconsistency in subjective expectations.
papers.ident: Theory-guided decomposition of yield sensitivity using survey expectations without imposing an expectation formation model.
papers.contribution: Derives a condition linking expected and realized rates that holds for arbitrary beliefs, allowing a decomposition of yield sensitivity into expectations and risk premia without assuming how expectations form.

papers.title: The security unlock: How rural social pension makes people more entrepreneurial?
papers.q: How does a rural social pension affect entrepreneurship?
papers.summary: Studies how a rural social pension makes people more entrepreneurial, according to the title.

papers.title: The Macroeconomic Effect of Stimulus Checks: Evidence from Postwar Veterans’ Payments

authors.inst: London School of Economics and Political Science

papers.q: Do one-off, deficit-financed stimulus checks boost consumption and the economy?
papers.summary: The payments produced a temporary rise in transfers and a persistent hump-shaped rise in consumption. The transfer multiplier reaches 1 after six months and exceeds 2 after a year, which the standard HANK model cannot match but a version with imperfect expectations can.
papers.ident: Natural experiment: exogenous postwar veterans' payments, with local projection-style responses and a HANK model with imperfect expectations.
papers.contribution: Uses payments to U.S. veterans after World War II, plausibly exogenous to the economy, as a natural experiment on stimulus checks and confronts a HANK model with the estimated consumption response.
papers.dataDetail: Postwar U.S. veterans' payments and consumption series.

papers.title: The Remains of the Trade: The U.S.–China Trade War and its Aftermath
papers.summary: Studies the U.S.-China trade war and its aftermath, according to the title.
papers.q: What are the consequences of the U.S.-China trade war and its aftermath?

papers.title: Measuring and Projecting U.S. Investment in Semiconductor Manufacturing Capacity
papers.q: How well do official and alternative data sources measure and project U.S. semiconductor fab investment?
papers.summary: Government sources face limitations for real-time tracking: their categories are too broad and publication lags are substantial. SEMI quarterly project-level data show broad consistency with official investment levels through 2023.
papers.conclusion: SEMI is a credible supplement to official statistics and the work is a case study in combining government and alternative data.
papers.contribution: Validates project-level SEMI data against official statistics as a timelier, more specific tracker of semiconductor manufacturing investment.
papers.ident: Descriptive: comparison of official statistics with SEMI project-level data on semiconductor fabs through 2023.
papers.dataDetail: SEMI quarterly fab project data and official U.S. statistics through 2023.

papers.title: Migration, Identity and Political Economy in a Globalizing World
papers.summary: Discusses how immigration-induced identity changes can explain right-wing populism and the realignment of voters along a socio-cultural rather than economic dimension. Notes that effects on group boundaries depend on immigrant and host characteristics and local context.
papers.conclusion: The paper highlights open questions and directions for future research.
papers.q: How does immigration change identity, and how do these changes shape the rise of right-wing populism and political realignment?
papers.contribution: Synthesizes social psychology and its economic formalization to derive predictions on how immigration changes self-identification and the categorization of others.
papers.ident: Theory: review synthesizing identity models and evidence on immigration and politics.

papers.title: When Tax Shields Shrink: Interest Deductibility Limitations and Corporate Innovation
papers.q: How did the 2017 TCJA limit on interest deductibility affect corporate innovation?
papers.summary: Affected firms patent significantly less than unaffected firms and narrow the technological scope of their portfolios, concentrated in exploitative patents. Cross-country evidence from staggered implementation of interest limitation rules confirms negative effects.
papers.contribution: Links interest deductibility limits to innovation, identifying the debt tax shield as an implicit subsidy for exploitative patenting.
papers.ident: DiD comparing firms affected and unaffected by TCJA interest limits, plus cross-country staggered adoption.
papers.dataDetail: Firm financials and patent records, U.S. and cross-country.

papers.title: Cooler Laws, Safer Workers: Evaluating California’s Heat Standard and Injury Reduction
papers.q: Did California's 2005 heat standard reduce work injuries?
papers.summary: The standard substantially reduces injuries in construction, agriculture and transportation. Effects increase with outside temperatures and are larger among younger workers.
papers.conclusion: The findings have clear implications for workplace safety policy debates.
papers.ident: Triple-differences exploiting California's 2005 heat standard across industries and temperature exposure.
papers.contribution: Evaluates California's heat standard with a triple-differences design on workers' compensation data.
papers.dataDetail: California workers' compensation administrative data.

papers.title: The Returns to International Migration in a Free Mobility Setting: Evidence from Austria and Germany
papers.q: What are the wage returns to international migration between Austria and Germany under free mobility?
papers.summary: Austrian migrants to Germany gain about 13% in daily wages relative to matched co-workers, German migrants to Austria about 4%, mainly reflecting higher average wages in Germany. Returns are largest for those who stay and zero or slightly negative for those returning within a year.
papers.ident: DiD comparing migrants with previous co-workers matched on pre-move employment, 2-4 years before the move.
papers.contribution: Combines linked origin and destination administrative data for five years after the move and uses previous co-workers as a comparison group in a DiD.
papers.dataDetail: Linked administrative data for Austria and Germany, five years after migration.

papers.title: Fiscal Populism and Monetary Policy Rules
papers.q: How does a history of populist regimes and fiscal monetization affect how central banks conduct monetary policy today?
papers.summary: Using data for many advanced and emerging economies since 1960, left-leaning populist regimes are linked to more central bank lending to government, which is associated with marked rises in inflation. Countries with such histories respond more strongly to deviations of inflation expectations from target, even controlling for past inflation.
papers.conclusion: Central banks operating in the shadow of past populist regimes need to send stronger signals of independence and commitment to price stability.
papers.contribution: Links past left-leaning populism and deficit monetization to the strength of present central bank responses to inflation expectations, interpreting it through experienced learning.
papers.ident: Panel regressions of central bank lending on populist regimes, and of monetary policy rule coefficients on past populism, since 1960.
papers.dataDetail: Advanced and emerging economies since 1960, central bank lending and inflation expectations.

papers.title: Digital (Killer?) Acquisitions
papers.q: Do acquisitions of startups by major technology firms suppress or promote innovation?
papers.summary: Most acquired startups hold no patents; innovation rises before acquisition, continues afterward only where further acquisitions follow, and falls back when they end. Acquired patents gain citations, and 31% of employees and 23% of inventors leave within a year, but stayers patent substantially more.
papers.conclusion: There is little evidence that acquisitions by digital incumbents suppress innovation in aggregate.
papers.ident: Event-study style comparison of innovation before and after acquisition against comparable patents, with a stylized selection model.
papers.contribution: Links patent and workforce data to 1,200 startup acquisitions by eight technology firms and proposes a selection model for the observed innovation patterns.
papers.dataDetail: 1,200 startup acquisitions by eight large technology firms, linked patent and workforce data.

papers.title: Markup Estimation Using Production and Demand Data: An Application to the U.S. Brewing Industry
papers.q: Do production-based and demand-based approaches give consistent markup estimates in the U.S. brewing industry?
papers.summary: Both methods give similar average markups and reveal a recent upward trend. Demand-based markups under competitive retail markets align with production-based estimates when downstream costs are accounted for.
papers.ident: Structural: production-function and demand-system markup estimation, combined through a production-based markup moment.
papers.contribution: Compares and combines production-side and demand-side markup estimation, using a production-based markup moment in place of conventional demand instruments.
papers.dataDetail: U.S. brewing industry production and demand data.

papers.title: Managing Procurement Auction Failure: Bid Requirements or Reserve Prices?
papers.q: Are bid requirements or reserve prices better at managing auction failure and procurement costs?
papers.summary: Reserve prices can reduce procurement costs and substantially lower failure probabilities relative to bid requirements, especially when entry costs are high or signals are informative. Bid requirements are more likely to produce zero entry.
papers.contribution: Compares bid requirements and reserve prices in a first-price auction model with endogenous entry.
papers.ident: Theory: first-price procurement auction with endogenous entry comparing two mechanisms.

papers.title: Threat and Assimilation: Evidence from Refugees in Germany

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.q: How does local threat shape refugees' cultural assimilation and economic integration in Germany?
papers.summary: Refugees assigned to more hostile regions converge faster to Germans' stated cultural preferences, but do not find jobs faster and see slower earnings growth. Hostility heightens threat perceptions and discrimination slows economic integration.
papers.ident: Quasi-random allocation of refugees across German regions, 2013-2016, compared by local threat index.
papers.contribution: Exploits the plausibly exogenous allocation of refugees across German regions, 2013-2016, with a threat index combining contemporaneous and historical local xenophobia.
papers.dataDetail: Representative refugee survey and administrative records, Germany, 2013-2016.

papers.title: The Content Moderator’s Dilemma: Removal of Toxic Content and Distortions to Online Discourse
papers.q: How does removing toxic tweets distort online discourse, and can rephrasing with LLMs reduce the distortion?
papers.summary: In 5 million U.S. political tweets, removing toxic tweets significantly alters semantic composition, comparable to removing 4 of 67 topics at random. The effect comes from topics often expressed in toxic form, and LLM rephrasing reduces toxicity while mitigating distortions.
papers.contribution: Proposes and validates a text-embedding method for measuring content-moderation-induced distortions, and an LLM rephrasing alternative to removal.
papers.ident: Descriptive: embedding-based measurement of semantic changes when toxic tweets are removed or rephrased.
papers.dataDetail: Representative sample of 5 million U.S. political tweets.

papers.title: Quantity Commitments in Multiunit Auctions: Evidence from Credit Event Auctions
papers.q: How do quantity commitments work in multiunit auctions?
papers.summary: Studies quantity commitments in multiunit auctions using credit event auctions, according to the title.

papers.title: Cash transfers and social preferences of children
papers.q: How do cash transfers affect children's social preferences?
papers.summary: Studies how cash transfers relate to the social preferences of children, according to the title.

papers.title: Carbon Prices, Forest Conservation and Reforestation in the Brazilian Amazon
papers.q: How much forest conservation and reforestation in the Brazilian Amazon would different carbon prices induce?
papers.summary: Land in the Brazilian Amazon is allocated between cattle ranching, which emits carbon through deforestation, and forest, which absorbs it, with productivities that vary across locations. Modest increases in carbon prices would lead Brazil to capture a significant amount of greenhouse gases over the next 30 years.
papers.contribution: Builds a spatial and dynamic model of efficient land allocation between cattle ranching and forest, with stochastic cattle prices and uncertain local productivities, as a benchmark for carbon-price policies.
papers.conclusion: Tropical forest management is an important contributor to climate change mitigation.
papers.ident: Structural: spatial dynamic land-allocation model with stochastic cattle prices and uncertain location-specific productivities, used for carbon-price counterfactuals

papers.title: Data, Privacy Laws and Firm Production: Evidence from the GDPR
papers.q: How does the GDPR affect firm production and data use?
papers.summary: Studies how privacy laws, specifically the GDPR, affect data and firm production, according to the title.

papers.title: Measurement error and peer effects in networks

authors.inst: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.summary: In the linear-in-means model, measurement error can inflate rather than attenuate peer effects, risking false positives. Based on identification results, the paper presents consistent GMM and 2SLS estimators illustrated by Monte Carlo simulation.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: identification and consistent GMM/2SLS estimation of peer effects with mismeasured regressors in networks.
papers.q: How does measurement error bias peer effect estimates in the linear-in-means network model?
papers.contribution: Shows the asymptotic bias depends on individual characteristics and network links, and that network structure can identify peer effects without external information.

papers.title: Revisiting Retirement and Social Security Claiming Decisions
papers.summary: Subjective beliefs substantially narrow claiming-age gaps across education and marital status groups: program beliefs alone account for 48.6% of the education gap and 75.1% of the marital status gap. Ignoring them overstates responses to a higher normal retirement age and understates fiscal savings.
papers.q: Why do even wealthy, long-lived Americans claim Social Security at the earliest age, and what does this mean for policy?
papers.contribution: Adds policy details and subjective beliefs about longevity and program rules to a rich forward-looking life-cycle model.
papers.ident: Structural: life-cycle model with subjective beliefs about longevity and program rules, estimated on U.S. claiming behavior.

papers.title: Feeling rich or looking rich? Self-perceived vs socially-perceived relative income
papers.q: How do self-perceived and socially-perceived relative income differ?
papers.summary: Contrasts self-perceived with socially-perceived relative income, according to the title.

papers.title: Fostering institutional trust and organ donation: Evidence from a randomized informational intervention in Tunisia
papers.q: Can an expert-led informational intervention increase organ donor registration by building institutional trust in Tunisia?
papers.summary: The intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive spillovers to the control group. It raises medical and legal knowledge, supportive religious beliefs and institutional trust, but not attitudes or social expectations, and effects are driven by male students and those with supportive families.
papers.ident: RCT at a Tunisian university randomizing an expert-led organ donation information session.
papers.contribution: Evaluates a video testimonial, doctor presentation and Q&A in a randomized trial at a Tunisian university.
papers.dataDetail: Students at a Tunisian university, registration records and survey.

papers.title: Geopolitical risk and inflation: The role of energy markets
papers.q: How do geopolitical risk shocks affect inflation and activity, and what role do energy markets play?
papers.summary: A GPR surprise associated with geopolitical macro shocks is on average contractionary and deflationary, while one associated with energy shocks is contractionary and inflationary. The identification is validated using heterogeneity in sector-level responses.
papers.contribution: Separates geopolitical shocks tied to energy disruptions from those tied to economic contractions using high-frequency and narrative sign restrictions on the GPR index and oil prices.
papers.ident: VAR with high-frequency and narrative sign restrictions on the GPR index and oil price comovement around selected episodes.
papers.dataDetail: Caldara-Iacoviello GPR index, oil prices, inflation and sector-level series.

papers.title: Prosecutor politics: The impact of election cycles on criminal sentencing in the era of rising incarceration
papers.summary: Election years raised per capita prison admissions by 3 percent, about 63,000 additional admissions, and months sentenced. Effects were concentrated in the South, stronger in Republican counties, and declined as public opinion softened.
papers.conclusion: Sentencing outcomes respond to voter preferences, so the politics of rising incarceration may matter as much as the policies.
papers.ident: Staggered timing of district attorney elections across states and counties, 1986-2006.
papers.q: Did district attorney election cycles raise criminal sentencing and prison admissions during the rise in U.S. incarceration?
papers.contribution: Exploits variation in district attorney election timing across nearly 40 states, roughly 1986-2006.
papers.dataDetail: State prison admissions and district attorney election timing, nearly 40 U.S. states, 1986-2006.

papers.title: Entry and Profits in an Aging Economy: The Role of Consumer Inertia
papers.q: How does population aging, through consumer inertia, contribute to fewer young firms and higher profit shares?
papers.summary: Younger households are significantly less inertial; as demand shifts to inertial consumers, entry gets harder, markups rise and share tilts to larger firms. Aging accounts for 20%-30% of the decline in young firms and rise in profits, supported by reduced-form evidence across states and products.
papers.ident: Quantitative: calibrated firm dynamics model with OLG consumers, plus reduced-form evidence across U.S. states and product categories.
papers.contribution: Develops a firm dynamics model with overlapping generations of consumers differing in inertia, quantifying a demand-side channel from aging.
papers.dataDetail: U.S. household purchase micro data and state-by-product evidence.

papers.title: Demographics, Wealth, and Global Imbalances in the Twenty-First Century
papers.q: How will population ageing change returns to wealth, wealth-to-GDP ratios and global imbalances over the twenty-first century?
papers.summary: The compositional effect of ageing on wealth-to-GDP is positive, large and heterogeneous across countries. The model predicts ageing will lower returns to wealth, raise wealth-to-GDP ratios and widen global imbalances, and the conclusions hold in a richer model with bequests, savings and tax-and-transfer responses.
papers.ident: Quantitative: OLG model disciplined by a sufficient statistic computed from population forecasts and household survey wealth profiles for 25 countries.
papers.contribution: Uses a sufficient-statistic approach, built on a measured compositional effect of ageing in twenty-five countries, to pin down general equilibrium outcomes in an overlapping generations model.
papers.dataDetail: Population forecasts and household survey data from twenty-five countries.

papers.title: Attention to the Macroeconomy

authors.inst: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.q: Which economic topics are top of mind for German households and firms, and how does having inflation top of mind shape expectations?
papers.summary: The likelihood that inflation is top of mind rises with its payoff relevance, but prior experiences also predict it, more so in inflationary periods. Having inflation top of mind predicts more information acquisition and expectations further from ex-ante benchmarks, at odds with goal-optimality.
papers.contribution: Measures top-of-mind topics in quarterly German household and firm panels, 2020-2024, to test goal-directed attention against experience-based determinants.
papers.ident: Descriptive: panel regressions of top-of-mind inflation on payoff relevance and prior experiences, and of expectations on top-of-mind status.
papers.dataDetail: Quarterly German household and firm survey panels, 2020-2024.

papers.title: On the spatial allocation of college seats: Human capital production and the distribution of skilled labor
papers.q: How does the spatial allocation of college seats shape human capital production and the distribution of skilled labor?
papers.summary: Studies the spatial allocation of college seats, human capital production and the distribution of skilled labor, according to the title.

papers.title: Filling in the gaps: Digital platform economies and the agglomeration of urban consumption amenities
papers.q: How do digital platform economies shape the agglomeration of urban consumption amenities?
papers.summary: Studies digital platform economies and the agglomeration of urban consumption amenities, according to the title.

papers.title: Media Slant is Contagious
papers.q: Does Fox News viewership shift the partisan slant of local U.S. newspapers?
papers.summary: Higher Fox News viewership causes local newspapers to adopt more right-wing slant over 1995-2008. The effect emerges gradually, several years after introduction, and appears driven mainly by changing local political preferences.
papers.ident: IV using Fox News channel positioning as instrument for viewership, with text-scaled newspaper slant, 1995-2008.
papers.contribution: Measures newspaper slant by scaling article texts to congressional speeches and uses channel positioning as an instrument for Fox News viewership.
papers.dataDetail: Local U.S. newspaper article texts and congressional speeches, 1995-2008.

papers.title: Heritability and Social Interaction in Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from the Population of Twins in the United States
papers.summary: Using 44,000 twin pairs in the 2000 Census linked to earnings 20 years later, log earnings show strong heritability (h2 about 0.36); both person and employer pay components are heritable. Heritability of employer premiums is driven mainly by same-sex twins working at the same firm, suggesting social interactions can inflate genetic estimates.
papers.ident: Extended twins design identifying heritability from DiD of same-sex versus opposite-sex twins versus siblings, with an AKM decomposition.
papers.q: How heritable are labor market outcomes, and do social interactions inflate genetic estimates?
papers.contribution: Extends the Classical Twins Design to settings without observed zygosity, identifying heritability from same-sex versus opposite-sex twins and siblings.
papers.dataDetail: 44,000 twin pairs in the 2000 Census linked to earnings 20 years later.

papers.title: Strategic Sovereignty: U.S.–Israeli Strikes and the Reversal of Anti-Regime Protest in Iran

authors.inst: École Supérieure des Sciences Économiques et Commerciales

papers.q: Did the 2026 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran redirect domestic protest from anti-government to pro-government mobilization?
papers.summary: Anti-government protest receded before the strikes amid repression and a foreign-agent narrative. After counties' first exposure to a strike, total protest changed little but shifted sharply from anti-government to pro-government, consistent with strategic sovereignty.
papers.conclusion: Overt foreign intervention can make domestic opposition easier to portray as externally aligned, weakening its legitimacy.
papers.ident: Staggered DiD exploiting the precise location and timing of counties' first exposure to U.S.-Israeli strikes in Iran, 2026.
papers.contribution: Combines high-frequency geocoded protest data with geocoded strike records, exploiting the location and staggered timing of counties' first strike exposure.
papers.dataDetail: Geocoded Iranian protest events and U.S.-Israeli strike records, 2026.

papers.title: The Macroeconomic Returns to School Finance Reforms: Micro-Calibrated Predictions Meet Causal Evidence
papers.summary: The simulation predicts little change for 10 to 15 years and gains reaching 7.8 percent after 60 years. State earnings per worker track this path, rising roughly 4.7 percent above counterfactual after 30 years, with GDP per capita also rising after an initial modest decline.
papers.ident: Staggered event study of school finance reforms across U.S. states, tested against a micro-calibrated cohort replacement simulation.
papers.contribution: Combines design-based micro estimates of reform effects with a cohort replacement simulation of state earnings, then tests the prediction in a staggered event study.
papers.q: Do state school finance reforms raise macroeconomic output as private earnings returns suggest?
papers.dataDetail: State-level earnings per worker and GDP per capita across U.S. states.

papers.title: Did COVID Change the Black Neighborhood Startup Deficit? Evidence from the Startup Cartography Project
papers.q: Did COVID change the Black neighborhood startup deficit?
papers.summary: A long-standing Black neighborhood startup deficit reverses sharply in 2020, especially where pre-existing deficits were larger. Relative entrepreneurship remains elevated in high-deficit neighborhoods, and neighborhood-oriented entrepreneurship remains elevated through 2024.
papers.contribution: Uses registration data from 38 states in the Startup Cartography Project to test a local poverty-trap interpretation of low entrepreneurship in Black neighborhoods.
papers.ident: Descriptive: neighborhood-level startup rates by racial composition before and after 2020.
papers.dataDetail: Business registration data from 38 U.S. states through 2024.

papers.title: When Resources Meet Relationships: The Returns to Personalized Supports for Low-Income Students
papers.q: Does Communities In Schools, which places coordinators in high-poverty schools, improve outcomes and earnings of low-income students?
papers.summary: The program boosts test scores for struggling students, and the gains persist into higher high school completion and adult earnings. Test scores explain only about half of the graduation effect, and students with different needs have comparable long-run gains.
papers.conclusion: Placing a trusted adult in schools, backed by a network of services, may be a scalable way to improve economic mobility.
papers.ident: Staggered DiD exploiting the rollout of Communities In Schools across schools.
papers.contribution: Exploits the staggered rollout of the largest U.S. personalized student support program, tracing effects from test scores to adult earnings.
papers.dataDetail: Linked school records and adult earnings data.

papers.title: Did the Affordable Care Act Save Lives?
papers.q: Did the Affordable Care Act, net of Medicaid expansions, reduce mortality?
papers.summary: Using NHIS Linked Mortality Files for nationally representative 40-58 year-olds, the paper applies DiD and triple-difference designs to estimate the effects of the ACA on mortality. The abstract text provided does not state the estimates.
papers.ident: DiD and triple-difference designs exploiting ACA coverage gains and Medicaid expansion variation.
papers.contribution: Proposes an empirical approach separating the ACA's effect net of Medicaid expansion, the incremental Medicaid effect and the overall effect on mortality.
papers.dataDetail: NHIS Linked Mortality Files, ages 40-58.

papers.title: Does Information Influence the Choice between Social Security Disability and Early Retirement Benefits?
papers.q: Does receiving Social Security information change the choice between disability and early retirement benefits?
papers.summary: Receiving the statement increases the probability of applying for both programs among people with a work-limiting condition or low work ability, especially those further from full retirement age. The rise in DI applications is split between DI-only and both-program applications.
papers.contribution: Examines how an initial Social Security statement with personalized benefit estimates affects applications for DI and OAI at ages 62 to full retirement age.
papers.ident: Comparison of individuals around receipt of an initial Social Security statement by health and age.

papers.title: (Mis)measuring Uncertainty: Bunching in Probabilistic Expectations

authors.inst: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.summary: Bunching is higher among less financially literate respondents and rises with panel tenure. Enforcing neutral interviewer protocols reduces it by about 15 percentage points and a questionnaire redesign by a further 18 points.
papers.conclusion: Degenerate responses can reflect task burden and survey administration, so standard measures overstate certainty and understate uncertainty.
papers.ident: Before-after comparison around changes in interviewer protocols and questionnaire design in two surveys.
papers.q: Does bunching in probabilistic expectation questions reflect genuine certainty or survey artifacts?
papers.contribution: Uses survey-design changes in the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and Spanish Survey of Household Finances to show bunching is partly an artifact.
papers.dataDetail: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and Spanish Survey of Household Finances.

papers.title: Food Labeling Policies: Aggregate Impacts and Heterogeneity Across Categories
papers.q: How did Chile's front-of-package food labeling policy affect consumer intake and firm reformulation?
papers.summary: Consumers reduced sugar and caloric intake by 9% and 6%. Labels prompt substitution within categories, stronger where labels give new information, and firms bunch at thresholds with substantial heterogeneity across categories.
papers.conclusion: Policy-response heterogeneity should be considered for effective policy design.
papers.ident: Before-after policy comparison of purchases plus bunching of products at regulatory nutrient thresholds in Chile.
papers.contribution: Estimates aggregate and category-level demand responses and supply-side bunching at regulatory thresholds for the Chilean labeling policy.
papers.dataDetail: Chilean consumer purchase and product nutrient data.

papers.title: Disappearing Dollar Convenience?
papers.q: Has the convenience yield on dollar safe assets disappeared over the last five years?
papers.summary: Within dollar assets, safe asset convenience yields in 2025 are about the same as in 2019 and expected to persist for a decade. Relative to safe assets of other currencies, the richness of U.S. dollar safe assets, particularly Treasurys, has fallen considerably; dollar repo has the highest convenience.
papers.conclusion: Dollar convenience persists for domestic liquidity purposes but has declined for global liquidity purposes.
papers.contribution: Measures the convenience yield on dollar safe assets over the last five years, domestically and across currencies.
papers.ident: Descriptive: measurement of convenience yields on dollar and foreign safe assets, 2019-2025.
papers.dataDetail: Yields on U.S. dollar and other-currency safe assets, 2019-2025.
