papers.q: What gains could traditional finance get from blockchain's data structure alone?
papers.contribution: Analyzes an idealized blockchain data structure with trust anchored in traditional sources and identifies three categories of improvement for existing transactions.
papers.summary: Gains come from reducing real resource costs, improving balance sheet efficiency and reducing intermediation rents. Potential gains could be significant, especially from reduced rents, though hard to quantify precisely.
papers.ident: Theory: conceptual framework with order-of-magnitude estimates.

papers.title: Targeting, Personalization, and Engagement in an Agricultural Advisory Service
papers.q: How should calls be targeted in an agricultural advisory service to raise engagement, and do targeted policies hold up over time?
papers.contribution: Runs iterative experiments for a service reaching over one million Indian farmers and uses off-policy evaluation on randomized call assignments plus on-policy tests.
papers.summary: Targeted policies raise engagement by up to 8% under off-policy evaluation on held-out data from the same period, but realized gains are substantially smaller when implemented in later weeks. The authors develop tools to diagnose the shortfall and adopt a transfer-learning approach that accounts for temporal shifts.
papers.ident: Randomized call assignments with off-policy and on-policy evaluation of targeting rules.
papers.dataDetail: Call and engagement records for over one million farmers in rural India.

papers.title: Work from Home and Fertility
papers.q: Does working from home raise fertility?
papers.summary: Lifetime fertility is greater by 0.32 children per woman globally (0.47 in the US) when both partners work from home one or more days a week. Among women 20-39, gaining WFH raises planned fertility by 0.15 child and losing it lowers planned fertility by 0.10.
papers.contribution: Uses three approaches: a 38-country Global Survey of Working Arrangements and a US survey, workers' reported planned fertility under WFH changes, and ACS data on changes in WFH availability.
papers.ident: Conditional correlations, planned fertility questions and changes in WFH availability in ACS data.
papers.dataDetail: Global Survey of Working Arrangements in 38 countries, a US survey and American Community Survey data for 2017-2024.

papers.title: AI in Science

authors.inst: Ollscoil na Gaillimhe – University of Galway

papers.q: How does AI affect the knowledge production function in science?
papers.summary: Knowledge production is decomposed into stages to describe the jagged frontier of AI, with differential returns across domains such as data-rich biology versus anomaly-sparse physics and across stages such as design aids versus question generation. Human judgment remains indispensable for abductive inference, contextual nuance and trade-offs in data-sparse settings.
papers.ident: Theory: task-based model of AI-augmented knowledge production.
papers.contribution: Characterizes AI as an augmentation tool for search over combinatorial spaces and builds a task-based model distinguishing ordinary from AI-expert scientists.

papers.title: max EPS Payout Policy
papers.summary: EPS maximizers retain cash when investment offers a higher yield and otherwise return it. Growth stocks face a higher hurdle, deep value stocks are most likely to distribute, and since only buybacks can be accretive, EPS-maximizing CEOs prefer buybacks to dividends.
papers.ident: Theory: EPS-maximizing payout model.
papers.q: What payout policy maximizes earnings per share, and why do EPS maximizers prefer buybacks?
papers.contribution: Derives the EPS-maximizing payout policy in which the cost of holding cash equals the firm's earnings yield.

papers.title: Noisy Foresight
papers.summary: Subjects often fail to plan at future contingencies, violating perfect foresight, and neither experience nor prompting helps. The best-fitting model has subjects expecting fewer mistakes when the utility consequences of future actions are more disparate.
papers.q: Do decision-makers think through their own future actions before making initial choices?
papers.contribution: Runs a controlled experiment in a one-player dynamic setting and compares five behavioral models of foresight.
papers.ident: Laboratory experiment on dynamic decisions with structural estimation of foresight models.
papers.dataDetail: Laboratory data on dynamic decision problems.

papers.title: Structural change in sub-Saharan Africa: An open economy perspective
papers.q: What drives structural change in sub-Saharan Africa from an open economy perspective?
papers.summary: Domestic and foreign sectoral TFP are important drivers of structural change, while trade integration over time plays a small role, though trade transmits foreign productivity trends. Similar calibrations are run for 11 developing Asian countries.
papers.ident: Quantitative: calibrated open economy structural change model.
papers.contribution: Calibrates an open economy structural change model with income, substitution and comparative advantage effects to 11 SSA countries and nine major economies using input-output tables, 2000-2018.
papers.dataDetail: Input-output tables for 11 SSA and 11 developing Asian countries, 2000-2018.

papers.title: Domestic wedges and the (in)sensitivity of CPI to exchange rates
papers.q: How do domestic wedges shape the sensitivity of consumer prices to exchange rates?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of domestic wedges and the insensitivity of CPI to exchange rates.

papers.title: Product Safety in the Age of AI: Autonomy, R&D, and Liability
papers.q: How should liability for products powered by AI be designed when autonomy, R&D and extreme risks matter?
papers.summary: Raising AI liability for ordinary loss above actual harm can reduce excessive autonomy and raise welfare even when it lowers R&D. A well-designed rule implements efficient autonomy and balanced R&D, but under targeted R&D to reduce extreme risk, full efficiency cannot be achieved with liability, and regulations limiting extreme risk can perform better.
papers.contribution: Studies optimal liability for AI-powered products with ordinary harms and extreme large-scale risks that make full liability impractical.
papers.ident: Theory: liability rules for AI product safety with autonomy and R&D choices.

papers.title: An empirical evaluation of some long-horizon macroeconomic forecasts
papers.q: How well do long-horizon macroeconomic forecasts perform empirically?
papers.summary: The title indicates an empirical evaluation of some long-horizon macroeconomic forecasts.

papers.title: Did the Cold War produce development clusters in Africa?
papers.q: Did the Cold War produce development clusters in Africa?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of whether the Cold War produced development clusters in Africa.

papers.title: The impact of public-private partnership health plans on private insurance
papers.q: How do public-private partnership health plans affect private insurance?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the impact of public-private partnership health plans on private insurance.

papers.title: Do markets deliver? Competition and Choice in European healthcare markets
papers.q: Have market-based reforms delivered better outcomes in European healthcare?
papers.summary: Over the last two decades European policy makers have introduced market mechanisms into previously heavily constrained healthcare environments. The paper examines whether they improved outcomes for patients or taxpayers and signals next steps for research.
papers.contribution: Synthesizes economic analyses of competition and choice reforms in European healthcare and highlights what is known and not known.

papers.title: Swiftness and Delay of Punishment
papers.q: How do the swiftness and delay of punishment affect compliance with speeding tickets?
papers.summary: Delays of four or more weeks lower timely payments by 7% to 9%, and very swift tickets sent within one or two days may raise timely payments. The findings align with predictions elicited from expert scholars in a survey.
papers.ident: Administrative bottlenecks creating delays and later randomized ticket processing speed.
papers.contribution: Exploits administrative delays at the launch of a speed-camera system and a later randomized assignment of tickets to swift or delayed processing.
papers.dataDetail: Administrative data from automated speed cameras and ticket payments.

papers.title: Firm networks and global technology diffusion
papers.q: How do firm networks drive global technology diffusion?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of firm networks and global technology diffusion.

papers.title: Estimation and inference for unbalanced panel data models with interactive fixed effects
papers.q: How can unbalanced panel data models with interactive fixed effects be estimated and tested?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of estimation and inference for unbalanced panel data models with interactive fixed effects.

papers.title: How do holistic wrap-around anti-poverty programs affect employment and individualized outcomes?
papers.summary: The treatment effect on employment three years after assignment is 9 ± 9 percentage points, and the effect on high housing quality after one year is -2 ± 12 points, both imprecise. Exploratory analysis points to additional evidence on other outcomes.
papers.ident: Randomized assignment of participants to wrap-around services or a control group.
papers.q: Do holistic wrap-around anti-poverty programs improve employment and individual outcomes?
papers.contribution: Runs a randomized controlled trial of Bridges to Success with two cohorts assigned to intensive services lasting about two years or to help with an immediate need, with pre-specified employment and non-employment outcomes.
papers.dataDetail: Two cohorts in the Bridges to Success program with employment records and surveys.

papers.title: Preferential credit policy with sectoral markup heterogeneity

authors.inst: University of International Business and Economics

papers.q: How does preferential credit policy work when sectoral markups are heterogeneous?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of preferential credit policy with heterogeneous sectoral markups.

papers.title: The US-China trade war creates jobs (elsewhere)
papers.q: Did the US-China trade war create jobs elsewhere?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of job creation elsewhere due to the US-China trade war.

papers.title: Local information, mismatch, and the cost of randomization in regulatory enforcement

authors.inst: University of International Business and Economics
University of International Business and Economics
Nanjing University of Finance and Economics

papers.q: How do local information and mismatch affect the cost of randomization in regulatory enforcement?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of local information, mismatch and the cost of randomization in regulatory enforcement.

papers.title: A traffic-jam theory of growth
papers.q: Can a traffic-jam mechanism explain growth?
papers.summary: The title indicates a theory of growth based on a traffic-jam mechanism.

papers.title: The crowding-in effects of local government debt in China

authors.inst: University of International Business and Economics
Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
Central University of Finance and Economics

papers.q: Does local government debt in China crowd in other investment?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the crowding-in effects of local government debt in China.

papers.title: The Changing Landscape of International Development: An Introduction

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research
Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.summary: Extreme poverty has declined and life expectancy, schooling and democracy have risen since the late 1980s, but poverty reduction has slowed, especially after COVID-19, amid conflict, fragility and climate risks. The introduction discusses how external conditions, state capacity and policy choices shape development and the shifting growth drivers.
papers.q: What drives and constrains international development in a changing global landscape?
papers.contribution: Takes stock of 15 chapters of Volume 6 of the Handbook of Development Economics on barriers to progress, future growth sources and shared growth.

papers.title: Measuring Payroll Employment: A Note on the Current Employment Statistics
papers.summary: CES revisions tend to be small but have increased in recent years. Ideas for improvement include expanding the sample with internal or external data, benchmarking more often and improving estimation of establishment births and deaths.
papers.q: How reliable is the Current Employment Statistics payroll series and why do its revisions matter?
papers.contribution: Provides a primer on CES methodology and analyzes recent survey response and data revision patterns.
papers.ident: Descriptive: analysis of survey response rates and revision patterns.
papers.dataDetail: BLS Current Employment Statistics and revision data.

papers.title: Imitation, Reciprocity, and Community Structure in Norm Transmission: Evidence from Teachers and Students
papers.q: How do teachers' rule violations in grading affect students' cheating?
papers.summary: Students are significantly more likely to cheat when teachers systematically undergrade them, consistent with imitation and negative reciprocity. When teachers systematically overgrade, responses vary by community structure.
papers.contribution: Uses administrative data on high-stakes exams, comparing internal teacher-assigned scores with externally graded national scores, with within-student variation in exposure to different teachers.
papers.ident: Within-student variation in exposure to teachers with different grading violations.
papers.dataDetail: Administrative data on teacher-assigned internal scores and national exam scores.

papers.title: The Market Value of Reproductive Rights: Evidence from U.S. Housing Markets
papers.q: What is the market value of reproductive rights as capitalized into US housing markets?
papers.summary: Total abortion bans reduced rents by 2.2% on average from July 2022 through June 2025, reaching 4.0% in the latest year, and raised rental vacancy rates by 1.1 percentage points, reaching 1.8. Estimates for home values and homeowner vacancy rates are similar but less precise.
papers.ident: Synthetic difference-in-differences comparing states with total abortion bans to others after Dobbs.
papers.contribution: Evaluates total abortion bans after the 2022 Dobbs decision with a synthetic difference-in-differences design using Zillow indices and Census vacancy data.
papers.dataDetail: Zillow housing market indices and Census Housing Vacancy Survey data, 2022-2025.

papers.title: When Incentives Aren't Enough: Evidence on Inattention and Imperfect Memory from HIV Medication Adherence
papers.q: Do reminders improve the effectiveness of financial incentives for HIV medication adherence?
papers.summary: Financial incentives alone raise adherence by 10.6 percentage points, while pairing incentives with reminders raises it by 24.3 points. Medication refill data support the model, in which reminders mitigate both frictions.
papers.ident: Randomized financial incentives with and without reminders.
papers.contribution: Runs a randomized trial in Mozambique and develops a model in which inattention and imperfect memory of payment eligibility reduce incentive effectiveness.
papers.dataDetail: HIV medication refill data in a randomized trial in Mozambique.

papers.title: Mergers and Non-contractible Benefits: The Employees' Perspective
papers.q: Do mergers reduce employees' satisfaction on non-contractible dimensions of work?
papers.summary: Controlling for pre-trends, mergers lower employee satisfaction, especially on non-contractible dimensions (about 6% of a standard deviation). The effect is stronger in target than acquiring firms, and text analysis links the decline to perceived breaches of implicit contracts.
papers.contribution: Combines Refinitiv merger events with web-scraped Glassdoor reviews to test the incomplete-contract prediction that acquisitions harm workers' non-contractible work experience.
papers.conclusion: Mergers may reduce workers' job utility through non-monetary channels.
papers.ident: Merger events compared with pre-trends in employee review satisfaction.
papers.dataDetail: Refinitiv M&A events and web-scraped Glassdoor reviews.

papers.title: Who Gets What in Education: Can School Matching Improve Student Achievement?
papers.q: Can school matching improve student achievement more than restructuring school portfolios?
papers.summary: Sophisticated reallocation policies that optimize student-school matches give modest gains, constrained by limited seats at effective schools. Replacing low-performing schools achieves comparable improvements with less disruption, and basic graduation rate metrics identify struggling schools.
papers.contribution: Estimates school effects with vertical quality and horizontal student-specific match components in New York City high schools to compare reallocation with resource augmentation.
papers.ident: Value-added models with vertical and horizontal match effects, plus analysis of school closures.
papers.dataDetail: New York City high school administrative data.

papers.title: When Do Financial Frictions Matter for Misallocation?
papers.q: When do financial frictions matter for capital misallocation?
papers.summary: Chinese manufacturing data show dispersed ARPK strongly related to borrowing costs, patterns absent in US data. Eliminating financial frictions raises TFP by 25 percentage points, but by less than 2 points without other capital distortions, because of interactions with permanent firm-level distortions.
papers.contribution: Builds a heterogeneous-firm model with endogenous firm-specific borrowing costs and exogenous capital wedges, disciplined by borrowing costs and average revenue product of capital.
papers.ident: Structural: heterogeneous-firm model matched to borrowing costs and ARPK dispersion.
papers.dataDetail: Chinese manufacturing firm-level data.

papers.title: Competition in Health Insurance Markets
papers.q: How do market power and adverse selection shape competition in US health insurance markets?
papers.summary: US private health insurance markets are highly concentrated and increasingly so. Empirical evidence confirms that insurer consolidation raises premiums, and antitrust, risk adjustment, regulation and informational interventions shape competition and consumer welfare.
papers.contribution: Documents concentration across commercial, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid markets and reviews how asymmetric information interacts with market power.

papers.title: How does AI Distribute the pie? Large Language Models and the Ultimatum Game.

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.q: How do large language models behave in the Ultimatum Game?
papers.summary: LLM behavior is heterogeneous but predictable given stakes and agent type. Rational profit-maximization and human-like choices occur, alongside a distinct altruistic mode of high offers that actually reflects acceptance risk.
papers.contribution: Studies LLM choices in the Ultimatum Game varying stakes, opponent type (human or AI) and role (Proposer or Responder).
papers.ident: Experimental variation in stakes, opponent type and role.
papers.dataDetail: LLM choices in Ultimatum Game experiments.

papers.title: Pricing Protection: Credit Scores, Disaster Risk, and Home Insurance Affordability
papers.summary: Credit scores affect premiums as much as disaster risk, with low-credit homeowners paying 24% more for identical coverage. The ban considerably weakens the link between credit score and pricing, and a low credit score raises premiums about as much as it raises mortgage rates.
papers.ident: Washington State ban on the use of credit information in insurance pricing.
papers.q: How much do credit scores affect homeowners insurance premiums relative to disaster risk?
papers.contribution: Links 70 million policies to mortgages and property-level disaster risk, and uses a Washington State ban on credit information in pricing as a natural experiment.
papers.dataDetail: 70 million insurance policies linked to mortgages and property-level disaster risk.

papers.title: The Micro-Geography of Persuasion: Randomized Peer Exposure and Legislative Outcomes
papers.summary: Closely seated peers shift votes by 11.9 percentage points, with the effect concentrated in the closest peers and dissipating beyond about 19.6 feet. Close peers also raise the probability of aisle-crossing, roughly eight times more on final votes on bills.
papers.ident: Random assignment of Senate seating and peer proximity.
papers.q: Do randomly assigned Senate seatmates influence each other's votes?
papers.contribution: Exploits random seat assignment in the US Senate and AI-enhanced computer vision on CSPAN video to measure physical peer proximity and its effect on voting.
papers.dataDetail: Senate roll-call votes and CSPAN video analyzed with computer vision every 10 seconds.

papers.title: Institutional Shocks and Migration Adjustment: Evidence from the Syrian Crisis and Brexit’s Referendum and Implementation
papers.summary: The 2016 referendum sharply lowered UK net migration relative to Germany, mainly through a contraction in immigration, and the 2021 end of free movement reinforced the decline in gross inflows. Countries more integrated into EU mobility networks before 2016 saw stronger contractions.
papers.ident: UK-Germany difference-in-differences around the 2016 referendum and 2021 end of free movement.
papers.q: How did Brexit and the Syrian crisis reshape migration through institutional shocks?
papers.contribution: Interprets Brexit as a two-stage institutional rupture and estimates a UK-Germany difference-in-differences model of net migration.
papers.dataDetail: Migration flows for the UK and Germany.

papers.title: The Effects of a Sudden Stop in Low-Skilled Immigration: Evidence from Korea’s Guest Worker Program
papers.q: What happens to firms when low-skilled immigrant labor supply is suddenly cut?
papers.contribution: Exploits South Korea's suspension of its guest worker program after the 2020 COVID-19 border closure, using firms' pre-pandemic reliance on immigrant labor.
papers.summary: The collapse in inflows increased firm exit, and surviving firms with greater dependence faced production disruptions and delays. Firms did not hire more domestic workers but reallocated Korean employees to lower-skilled tasks, causing occupational downgrading and wage declines.
papers.ident: Policy-driven variation in firms' pre-pandemic reliance on immigrant labor after the suspension.
papers.dataDetail: Korean firm and worker data around the 2020 guest worker suspension.

papers.title: Pay Now, Buy Never: The Economics of Consumer Prepayment Schemes
papers.q: Do firms profit from unused balances in consumer prepayment programs?
papers.summary: About 40% of prepaid value is never used, so merchants recover far more than the bonus cost, with a median firm earning roughly $5.5 in breakage profit per $1 of bonus credit. Participation modestly raises consumer spending, but firms gain much more from breakage than from loyalty-driven revenue.
papers.contribution: Analyzes a large Pay Now, Buy Later program using transaction data on over 4 million consumers.
papers.dataDetail: Transaction data on over 4 million consumers in a restaurant prepayment program.

papers.title: Repression
papers.q: Why do states repress and how should repression be studied?
papers.summary: The framework interprets two stylized facts: repression is higher in autocracies and has declined since the 1990s. It also covers under-researched aspects such as migration restrictions, targeting and backlash, and flags the challenges of judging success and of selection in measures of repression.
papers.contribution: Develops a conceptual framework of political repression built on the notion of the political project.

papers.title: Competition and the Phillips curve
papers.q: Does rising market concentration help explain the flattening of the Phillips curve?
papers.contribution: Extends the New Keynesian model with markup changes caused by entry and exit, under homothetic single aggregator demand systems that include CES and Translog.
papers.summary: The Phillips curve has flattened while concentration and markups have risen, and the paper asks whether the two are causally related. The single aggregator summarizes the effects of market concentration on the pricing behavior of monopolistically competitive firms.
papers.ident: Theory: New Keynesian model with entry, exit and variable markups under homothetic single aggregator demand.

papers.title: From childhood abduction to adulthood: Enduring consequences for women in Uganda
papers.q: What are the enduring consequences of childhood abduction for women in Uganda?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the long-run consequences of childhood abduction for women in Uganda.

papers.title: Global Value Chains and Labour Standards: The Race-to-the-Bottom Problem
papers.q: How does globalisation affect governments' incentives to set labour standards in global value chains?
papers.summary: Lower trade costs or adding countries with complementary skills improve working conditions, whereas adding countries with similar skills has the opposite effect. Equilibrium standards are stricter than optimal because countries pass some costs to others, and Nash equilibrium tariffs make regulation redundant until multilateral tariff cuts bring it back.
papers.contribution: Develops a stylised global value chain model of how trade costs and the addition of countries shape labour standards set by employers or governments.
papers.ident: Theory: stylised global value chain model with Nash equilibrium standards and tariffs.

papers.title: Making a Swap: Network Formation with Increasing Marginal Costs
papers.summary: Stable graphs feature assortativity and clustering, with conditions leading to hierarchies and cliquish behavior. The results map interpretable properties of preferences to network structures.
papers.q: Which networks can be stable when linking costs are increasing and players differ vertically?
papers.contribution: Proposes a general theory of strategic network formation with increasing marginal linking costs and vertical heterogeneity, characterizing the set of stable graphs without parametric assumptions.
papers.ident: Theory: revealed-preference characterization of stable graphs.

papers.title: Polygamy, co-wives’ complementarities, and intrahousehold inequality
papers.contribution: Develops and estimates a theory of polygamy in which co-wives interact in a senior-junior hierarchy.
papers.summary: In equilibrium single, monogamous and polygamous households emerge, and optimal female sorting generates co-wife inequality, with high-skilled women becoming senior wives of wealthy men and low-skilled juniors. Absent better outside options from marriage, banning polygamy harms all women.
papers.q: How do senior-junior co-wife complementarities shape polygamy and what happens if polygamy is banned?
papers.conclusion: Banning polygamy harms all women in the absence of better outside options.
papers.ident: Structural: estimated equilibrium matching model of marriage with senior-junior co-wives.

papers.title: Blackwell-Monotone Updating Rules
papers.summary: Bayes's law is strictly Blackwell monotone and is the only such rule among signal-independent distortions of Bayesian posteriors. If decisions are evaluated according to the agent's beliefs, Blackwell-monotone rules are affine distortions of Bayesian posteriors.
papers.q: Which belief updating rules ensure that more information is always better for the agent?
papers.contribution: Defines Blackwell-monotone updating rules and characterizes them within the class of signal-independent distortions of Bayesian posteriors.
papers.ident: Theory: characterization of Blackwell-monotone updating rules.

papers.title: Does $1 matter? Health care demand response to a small copayment
papers.q: Does a $1 copayment change health care demand?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of how health care demand responds to a small copayment of $1.

papers.title: Violence against journalists and freedom of the press: Evidence from Mexico
papers.q: How does violence against journalists affect freedom of the press in Mexico?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of violence against journalists and freedom of the press in Mexico.

papers.title: Transfer price documentation rules and multinational firm behavior – Evidence from France

authors.inst: German Institute of Development and Sustainability

papers.q: How do transfer price documentation rules change multinational firm behavior in France?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the effects of transfer price documentation rules on multinational firm behavior in France.

papers.title: Trade, storage, and climate extremes: Theory and evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa
papers.q: How do trade, storage and climate extremes interact in Sub-Saharan Africa?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study combining theory and evidence on trade, storage and climate extremes in Sub-Saharan Africa.

papers.title: Love thy neighbour? Violent armed conflict and trust: Evidence from Ethiopia
papers.q: How does exposure to violent conflict affect trust among young adults in Ethiopia?
papers.contribution: Uses novel individual-level conflict exposure data collected through audio computer-assisted self-interviewing.
papers.summary: Greater exposure lowers trust in neighbourhood residents but has no significant effect on generalized trust or trust in other neighbourhoods, across men, women and ethnic groups. Low exposure may raise local trust while high exposure substantially lowers it.
papers.dataDetail: Individual-level survey of young adults in Ethiopia with audio self-interviewing on violence exposure.

papers.title: Procurement with manipulation
papers.q: Do procuring administrations manipulate contract values to avoid regulatory thresholds, and with what effects?
papers.summary: Manipulation is substantial below the thresholds, mainly by administrations led by appointed rather than elected officials. It increases use of restricted auctions, reducing bidders, work length, delays and cost overruns, and increases repeated awards to less financially risky suppliers.
papers.ident: Bunching below regulatory thresholds, cross-validated with a reform that lowered thresholds.
papers.contribution: Uses bunching estimators on Italian public works data to document manipulation below thresholds that limit discretion and estimate its effects.
papers.dataDetail: Italian public works procurement data.

papers.title: Inflation vs Inclusion: Stabilization Policy in the Wake of the Pandemic
papers.q: How did policy manage the trade-off between inflation and an inclusive recovery after the pandemic?
papers.summary: A protracted stimulus fosters a more inclusive recovery but risks inflation that erodes workers' real income. The trade-off was unusually difficult because policy was squeezed between constraints, and inflationary pressures arose from joint monetary and fiscal stimulus, either alone producing milder price dynamics.
papers.ident: Quantitative: macro model of the US economy with counterfactual policy experiments.
papers.contribution: Embeds the inflation-inclusion trade-off in a quantitative model of the US economy with a zero lower bound and capacity constraints, and contrasts actual policy with counterfactuals.

papers.title: How Does the Earned Income Tax Credit Work? Exploring the Role of Commuting and Personal Transportation
papers.q: How does the Earned Income Tax Credit work through commuting and personal transportation?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the role of commuting and personal transportation in how the Earned Income Tax Credit works.

papers.title: Farmer Adoption and Payment Design Under Risk: Variability in Soil Carbon Sequestration Across Conservation Practices
papers.q: What carbon payments would induce farmers to adopt soil conservation practices under sequestration risk?
papers.summary: Required payments range from $8 per ton of carbon per year on well-drained soils to $32 on poorly drained soils, pointing to spatially targeted incentives. Risk in sequestration affects farmer choices.
papers.contribution: Builds an infinite-horizon dynamic optimization model of farmers' adoption of no-till and reduced tillage under payments tied to soil organic carbon accumulation, with risk in sequestration outcomes.
papers.ident: Structural: infinite-horizon dynamic optimization of adoption under risk.
papers.dataDetail: Soil type and sequestration variability data.

papers.title: Improving Organ Procurement Operations
papers.q: How do organ procurement organizations' approach decisions affect organ availability?
papers.summary: The model has the organization estimate probabilities of authorization and transplant, then apply a cost-benefit rule to decide whether to approach. It is used to study how these decisions affect the availability of organs for transplant in the United States.
papers.ident: Structural: separate identification of beliefs, preferences and true probabilities in the approach decision.
papers.contribution: Develops a structural econometric model of the decision to approach a potential donor's family, separately identifying the organization's beliefs, preferences and the true probabilities of authorization and transplant.

papers.title: Geoeconomic Competition and Capital Reallocation in Global FX Funding
papers.q: How does geoeconomic competition reallocate capital in the global FX funding market?
papers.summary: FX funding through swaps provides high-frequency measures of capital reallocation as countries compete through policy actions that shift returns or funding costs. Common shocks and strategic interactions make bilateral influence hard to identify.
papers.ident: Identification of funding fronts to separate bilateral influence from common shocks.
papers.contribution: Measures how one country's FX funding inflow responds to another country's actions, called reallocation exposure, by identifying funding fronts.
papers.dataDetail: High-frequency FX swap funding data.

papers.title: Multidimensional Signaling and the Rise of Cultural Politics
papers.summary: Less popular types try to pool with more popular ones while the more popular separate themselves. If cultural signals are more precise, politicians signal more there even when the economy matters more to voters, and the unpopular type benefits from the resulting conformity.
papers.q: Why does campaign rhetoric shift toward cultural issues when political labels become uninformative?
papers.contribution: Offers a model in which politicians signal their preferences on multiple dimensions through campaign rhetoric, with voters of limited information processing.
papers.ident: Theory: multidimensional signaling model with pooling and separating equilibria.

papers.title: Equity Financing and Exports: Evidence from IPO Approvals in China
papers.contribution: Compares exports of successful Chinese IPO applicants with near-miss applicants rejected at final review, excluding rejections that cite revenue or profitability concerns.
papers.summary: The first empirical analysis of how equity financing affects firm exports uses the regulatory approval of IPOs in China to ensure only qualified firms reach the final review. A cohort-based difference-in-differences analysis compares the two groups.
papers.ident: Cohort-based difference-in-differences comparing IPO approvals with near-miss rejections.
papers.q: Does access to equity financing raise firm exports?
papers.dataDetail: Chinese IPO final review records and firm export data.

papers.title: The Economics of Tariffs
papers.summary: Trade acts like a production technology improvement that creates aggregate gains but winners and losers within countries. Large countries can improve their terms of trade with tariffs, though if all do so they can end up worse off than under cooperative liberalization.
papers.q: What does economics say about the effects and justifications of tariffs?
papers.contribution: Reviews the economics of tariffs, covering gains from trade, terms-of-trade motives, redistribution and arguments based on externalities or national security.

papers.title: Consumption Wedges: Measuring and Diagnosing Distortions
papers.q: Can consumption wedges diagnose which distortions explain deviations from the frictionless consumption-savings model?
papers.summary: Different distortions imply different wedge properties, so wedges help to distinguish between models. The expectations data separate wedges due to frictions and behavioral preferences from those due to deviations from full-information rational expectations.
papers.contribution: Develops a sufficient-statistics approach to measure individual-level wedges between observed and frictionless consumption, using administrative transactions linked to surveyed expectations.
papers.ident: Sufficient statistics: wedges between observed and counterfactual frictionless consumption.
papers.dataDetail: Administrative transactions data linked to surveyed expectations for middle-income, low-liquidity US consumers.

papers.title: How Do Interest Rates Affect Consumption? Household Debt and the Role of Asset Prices
papers.q: How do interest rate cuts affect consumption through household debt and asset prices?
papers.summary: A 1pp reduction in mortgage rates raises consumption by 3% over the following six months. Consumption increases mostly because households borrow against higher house prices, with lower debt service mattering less.
papers.ident: Expiry of fixed-rate mortgages and variation in how house prices respond to rate cuts.
papers.contribution: Uses expiries of fixed-rate mortgages in administrative UK data to construct six million household-level natural experiments.
papers.conclusion: Monetary policy affects consumption largely through asset prices and borrowing.
papers.dataDetail: Administrative UK data on mortgages and consumption.

papers.title: Loneliness, Mental Health and the Work-From-Home Revolution
papers.summary: Teleworkable workers saw large and persistent increases in remote working, but adverse relative changes in loneliness and mental health symptoms during the pandemic had disappeared by 2023.
papers.ident: Difference-in-differences between workers in teleworkable and non-teleworkable occupations in 2019.
papers.q: Did the rise of remote work cause lasting increases in loneliness and poor mental health?
papers.contribution: Compares teleworkable and non-teleworkable workers in UKHLS panel data with difference-in-differences estimators.
papers.conclusion: Adverse effects were transitory in the UK.
papers.dataDetail: UK Household Longitudinal Study (UKHLS) panel data.

papers.title: Bubbles, Booms and Crashes in the US Stock Market 1792-2024
papers.q: How often do bubbles, booms and crashes occur in the US stock market?
papers.summary: Bubbles, defined as a large boom followed by a crash that reverses prior gains, are extremely rare. Booms do not reliably predict crashes but do predict higher subsequent volatility, raising the likelihood of both large gains and large losses.
papers.contribution: Examines US market booms, crashes and bubbles from 1792 to 2024 with aggregate and industry-level data, and replicates Greenwood, Shleifer and You (2019) on Cowles data for 1871-1938.
papers.ident: Descriptive: historical frequency of booms, crashes and bubbles.
papers.dataDetail: US aggregate market and industry portfolio data, 1792-2024, including Cowles Commission data.

papers.title: Interest Rate Risk and Cross-Sectional Effects of Micro-Prudential Regulation
papers.q: How do banks' interest rate exposure and uninsured deposits create run risk and how does micro-prudential regulation respond?
papers.summary: The model replicates empirical patterns such as the concentration of uninsured deposits in larger banks. Tighter capital requirements significantly lower run risk, and higher liquidity requirements on uninsured deposits do so efficiently if met exclusively with reserves.
papers.ident: Quantitative: heterogeneous-bank model with endogenous run risk.
papers.contribution: Develops a model of heterogeneous banks with endogenous run risk and joint portfolio and funding choices, and evaluates microprudential tools after rate hikes.

papers.title: A Quantitative Theory of Domestic Outsourcing: The Role of Wage-Proportional Staffing Fees
papers.summary: Staffing fees proportional to wages lower returns to human capital, so outsourced workers under-invest. Despite that, total utility is higher with unrestricted outsourcing than without it, though mild restrictions are examined.
papers.q: What are the trade-offs of domestic outsourcing with wage-proportional staffing fees?
papers.contribution: Builds a directed search model with endogenous human capital investment and sorting into outsourced and non-outsourced jobs.
papers.ident: Quantitative: directed search model with endogenous human capital and sorting.

papers.title: AI, Human Cognition and Knowledge Collapse
papers.q: How does agentic AI affect human learning incentives and the long-run stock of shared knowledge?
papers.summary: Agentic AI gives context-specific recommendations that substitute for human effort, while a richer stock of general knowledge complements effort. The model highlights a sharp dynamic tension, with a learning externality from public signals.
papers.ident: Theory: dynamic learning model with complementary general and context-specific knowledge.
papers.contribution: Builds a dynamic model where decisions combine community-level general knowledge with individual context-specific knowledge, and learning produces both a private and a thin public signal.

papers.title: What Threshold Should be Applied to Tests of Factor Models?
papers.q: What significance threshold should be used when testing factor models after many factors have been examined?
papers.summary: The framework implies a t-statistic cutoff of at least 3.0. The local False Discovery Rate is advocated because it gives the probability that the null is true for a given test statistic.
papers.contribution: Develops a framework that accounts for dependence across tests, the null distribution and sample-selection bias without assuming the total number of tests, giving a lower bound on valid thresholds.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: multiple testing with dependence, null specification and selection bias.

papers.title: Are Macro Shocks Second Order?
papers.q: Are macroeconomic shocks large enough to matter for the economy's course and welfare?
papers.summary: The economy is buffeted by calibrated TFP and capital depreciation shocks. Findings suggest macro shocks are second order for aggregate variability and for welfare.
papers.ident: Quantitative: large-scale stochastic OLG model with TFP and depreciation shocks.
papers.contribution: Solves a large-scale stochastic general equilibrium overlapping-generations model with 80 generations and 81 state variables using Marcet's projection method.
papers.conclusion: Macro shocks are second order.

papers.title: Redistribution Through Efficiency: Theory and Evidence from Three Electricity Markets
papers.q: How do efficiency improvements such as storage redistribute surplus in electricity markets?
papers.contribution: Uses micro-data on over 160 million bids from three electricity markets and derives price-theory results linking convexity of market excess demand to consumer benefits.
papers.summary: Consumer benefits arise from changes in general price levels rather than from stabilized prices. Convexity of excess demand, derived from the bids, strongly predicts consumer benefits across all markets, and even small allocative improvements can redistribute substantial surplus.
papers.ident: Theory: price-theory results with convexity of excess demand measured from bids.
papers.dataDetail: Over 160 million bids to buy and sell in three electricity markets.

papers.title: Fossil Fuels and Renewable Energy: Mix or Match?

authors.inst: Centro de Estudios Monetarios y Financieros
Centro de Estudios Monetarios y Financieros

papers.q: How does technology ownership across fossil and renewable sources affect pricing and efficiency in electricity markets?
papers.contribution: Develops a theoretical model of multi-unit auctions with cost heterogeneity and privately known capacities and simulates it with Spanish electricity market data.
papers.summary: Diversified firms compete more vigorously than specialized ones. Specialized firms are more productively efficient, but only when thermal sources dominate.
papers.ident: Theory: multi-unit auction model with cost heterogeneity, assessed by simulation.
papers.dataDetail: Spanish electricity market data.

papers.title: Who benefits from a maternity leave extension? Evidence from Chile
papers.q: Who benefits from a maternity leave extension in Chile?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of who benefits from a maternity leave extension in Chile.

papers.title: Statistical inference of optimal allocations I: Regularities and their implications
papers.q: What regularities and implications arise in statistical inference on optimal allocations?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of statistical inference on optimal allocations and the regularities and implications involved.

papers.title: Preferred habitats and timing in the world’s safe asset
papers.q: How do preferred habitats and timing matter in the market for the world's safe asset?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of preferred habitats and timing in the world's safe asset market.

papers.title: Optimal Decision Rules When Payoffs are Partially Identified
papers.summary: Rules can be implemented with the bootstrap and quasi-Bayesian methods in parametric and semiparametric settings. Applications cover treatment choice and optimal pricing, in realistic settings where finite-sample optimal rules are intractable.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: optimal decision rules under partial identification.
papers.q: What decision rules are asymptotically optimal when payoffs depend on a partially identified parameter?
papers.contribution: Derives asymptotically optimal statistical decision rules for discrete choice problems, combining a minimax approach for the partially identified parameter with average risk minimization for the point-identified one.

papers.title: Temporary Layoffs, Loss-of-Recall, and Cyclical Unemployment Dynamics
papers.q: Does loss-of-recall from temporary layoffs destabilize cyclical unemployment?
papers.summary: Workers in temporary-layoff unemployment lose their job permanently, which destabilizes the business cycle. The structural model captures pre- and post-pandemic dynamics and shows the Paycheck Protection Program produced sizable employment gains, partly by reducing loss-of-recall.
papers.ident: Structural: quantitative model of worker flows with temporary-layoff unemployment.
papers.contribution: Quantifies a countercyclical loss-of-recall effect in the data and develops a quantitative model with flows across employment, temporary-layoff and jobless unemployment.

papers.title: Sequential Cursed Equilibrium
papers.q: How should players who neglect information from hypothetical events be modeled in extensive-form games?
papers.summary: Players neglect information from hypothetical events but make inferences from observed events. The concept modifies the cursed equilibrium of Eyster and Rabin (2005).
papers.contribution: Proposes an extensive-form solution concept that modifies cursed equilibrium so players can be cursed about endogenous information.
papers.ident: Theory: extensive-form solution concept based on cursed equilibrium.

papers.title: What You Don’t Know May Be Good for You

authors.inst: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.q: Can providing information about expert outcomes reduce welfare?
papers.summary: Information can lead to inefficient matches because experts reject risky clients to build their reputation, so welfare can fall. Withholding information mitigates these incentives at the cost of misallocating experts known to be inept.
papers.contribution: Studies an economy where long-lived experts choose which client types to match with, and analyzes releasing outcome information such as medical report cards.
papers.ident: Theory: reputation model of expert-client matching.

papers.title: Immigration, Innovation, and Growth
papers.q: Does immigration raise innovation and wages across US counties?
papers.contribution: Proposes an identification strategy interacting quasi-random variation in county ancestry composition with contemporaneous migrant inflows, and estimates a structural model of endogenous growth and migration.
papers.summary: Immigration has a positive causal impact on local innovation and wages at the five-year horizon, dominating the short-run negative labor supply effect. Increased immigration since 1965 may have raised innovation and wages by 5 percent.
papers.ident: Shift-share type instrument interacting county ancestry composition with migrant inflows by origin country.
papers.dataDetail: US county-level data on immigration, innovation and wages.

papers.title: Reserve Price Signaling With Public Information: Evidence From Online Auto Auctions
papers.q: How does reserve price signaling affect seller payoffs and sale probability in auctions?
papers.contribution: Builds an auction model where the reserve price signals private quality information, estimates it on a large online auto auction platform, and simulates secret reserve prices.
papers.summary: The signaling incentive lowers the seller's payoff and probability of sale. A secret reserve price could shut down signaling and improve both, supporting its common use.
papers.ident: Structural: signaling auction model estimated on platform data with counterfactual simulations.
papers.dataDetail: Novel dataset from a large online auto auction platform.

papers.title: Externalities of climate adaptation in common-pool groundwater resources
papers.q: What externalities arise from climate adaptation in common-pool groundwater resources?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of externalities from climate adaptation in common-pool groundwater resources.

papers.title: The informativeness of combined experimental and observational data under dynamic selection
papers.q: Can short-term experiments combined with long-term observational data identify effects under dynamic selection?
papers.contribution: Studies identification of the average treatment effect on the treated survivors without long-term experimental data, using long-term observational data.
papers.summary: Informative bounds are impossible without model restrictions or auxiliary data. Combining short-term experimental data with observational data can overturn this negative result.
papers.ident: Econometric theory: bounds on ATETS combining experimental and observational data.

papers.title: Greening to grow: Evidence from environmental regulation and industrial firm productivity in China

authors.inst: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

papers.q: Does environmental regulation raise industrial firm productivity in China?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the relationship between environmental regulation and industrial firm productivity in China.

papers.title: Do the rich substitute political giving for charitable giving?
papers.q: Do the rich substitute political giving for charitable giving?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of whether wealthy individuals substitute political giving for charitable giving.

papers.title: Identification of Time-Inconsistent Models: The Case of Insecticide-Treated Nets
papers.summary: Using data from an insecticide-treated nets intervention in rural Odisha, India, about two-thirds of the sample are time-inconsistent agents. Population type probabilities and preferences are point-identified for time-consistent and sophisticated agents, with sharp set-identification for the others.
papers.q: Can time-inconsistent agents be identified in dynamic choice data, as in take-up of insecticide-treated nets?
papers.contribution: Formulates a dynamic discrete choice model with unobserved heterogeneity and possibly time-inconsistent agents and provides identification results for time-consistent, sophisticated, naive and partially sophisticated types.
papers.ident: Structural: identification of types in a dynamic discrete choice model with time-inconsistency.
papers.dataDetail: Insecticide-treated nets health intervention in rural Odisha, India.

papers.title: Optimal Refund Mechanism With Consumer Learning
papers.q: What refund mechanism is optimal when a buyer learns their valuation over time?
papers.summary: The seller either deters learning with a low price and no returns, or encourages maximal learning with a high price and free returns. Free returns are optimal only for intermediate prior beliefs.
papers.contribution: Studies simple and stochastic return policies and shows the optimal refund mechanism is deterministic.
papers.ident: Theory: optimal mechanism design with buyer learning.

papers.title: On the optimality of deferred public annuities
papers.q: When is it optimal to defer public annuities?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of the optimality of deferred public annuities.

papers.title: Breadwinner’s Burden: The Effect of Financial Concerns on Sleeplessness
papers.summary: Eligible household heads surveyed just after the transfer report a 0.4 standard deviation improvement in sleep quality and perform better on cognitive tasks sensitive to sleep deprivation. They also increase savings, reduce debts and feel less worried, frustrated and tired, with no effects for ineligible heads or other members.
papers.ident: Regression discontinuity in survey timing around an unconditional cash transfer disbursement.
papers.q: Do financial concerns affect breadwinners' sleep?
papers.contribution: Uses a regression discontinuity around the timing of an unconditional cash transfer in Indonesia to compare household heads surveyed just after versus just before disbursement.
papers.dataDetail: Household survey in Indonesia around an unconditional cash transfer.

papers.title: Rational Inattention during a Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.contribution: Introduces an information provision experiment into a dynamic rational inattention model and derives analytical results on how treatment effects vary with the environment and the individual.
papers.summary: The results are used to interpret findings in the empirical literature on information provision experiments that rational inattention of survey respondents can explain, and what this implies about behavior outside the survey.
papers.ident: Theory: dynamic rational inattention model with an information treatment.
papers.q: How does rational inattention shape treatment effects in information provision experiments?

papers.title: Inference for welfare metrics
papers.q: How can inference be conducted for welfare metrics?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of statistical inference for welfare metrics.

papers.title: Stability and resilience of alliances: A network approach
papers.q: What makes alliances stable and resilient?
papers.contribution: Characterizes alliance stability and resilience using graph-theoretic concepts in node- and edge-weighted networks with positive externalities among allies and negative ones with adversaries.
papers.summary: Resilience of alliances and their members is related to the members' core numbers within the alliance-induced subnetwork. The paper then analyzes strategic stability when members choose externality magnitudes through costly contributions.
papers.ident: Theory: graph-theoretic characterization of alliance stability using core numbers.

papers.title: The international transmission of asset market shocks in liquidity traps
papers.summary: Shocks to the supply or demand of assets have very different spillovers for an economy in a liquidity trap. A fall in the supply of assets issued abroad creates an asset shortage at home, which lowers the nominal rate and stimulates output in normal times but causes deflation, appreciation and possibly recession in a liquidity trap.
papers.q: How do asset market shocks spread internationally when an economy is in a liquidity trap?
papers.contribution: Builds a two-country heterogeneous-agent non-Ricardian model with asset scarcity and financial frictions in international capital markets.
papers.ident: Theory: two-country heterogeneous-agent model with asset scarcity.

papers.title: Drivers of Dollar Share in Foreign Exchange Reserves
papers.q: What drives changes in the dollar share of foreign exchange reserves?
papers.contribution: Provides a decomposition separating shifts in preferences for dollar assets from changes in reserve balances driven by countries whose allocations differ from the aggregate.
papers.summary: The concentrated nature of reserve holdings lets countries contributing a large share of aggregate reserves strongly influence the aggregate dollar share over time. In recent periods, the key contributors to preference shifts for dollar assets are changes in bilateral trade with the United States.
papers.ident: Descriptive: decomposition of aggregate dollar share changes into preference and balance channels.
papers.dataDetail: Official foreign exchange reserve portfolio data of central banks.

papers.title: Smartphones, Online Music Streaming, and Traffic Fatalities
papers.q: Do smartphones and music streaming increase traffic fatalities?
papers.summary: Music streaming rises by nearly 40% on release dates, while US traffic fatalities increase by nearly 15% on those same dates.
papers.ident: Event study on arbitrarily timed major music album releases.
papers.contribution: Uses event study analysis around major music album releases, when smartphone use likely surges, to causally assess smartphone distraction.
papers.dataDetail: Music streaming data and US traffic fatality records on album release dates.

papers.title: The Winners and Losers of Climate Policies: A Sufficient Statistics Approach

authors.inst: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

papers.q: Who wins and loses from climate policies such as carbon taxes, renewable subsidies and carbon tariffs?
papers.summary: The sufficient statistics depend on observables and identifiable elasticities such as the energy mix, energy rents, trade shares, supply and demand elasticities and damage parameters. Climate change has non-trivial reallocation effects through international trade.
papers.ident: Sufficient statistics: first-order welfare decomposition in an integrated assessment model.
papers.contribution: Expresses welfare changes under different policy regimes to the first order as sufficient statistics in a simple integrated assessment model with heterogeneous countries and trade in goods and energy.

papers.title: Why has Decreasing Schooling Inequality Not Led to Decreasing Earnings Inequality in South Africa?
papers.q: Why has falling schooling inequality in South Africa not reduced earnings inequality?
papers.summary: Changes in the distribution of education would on their own have significantly reduced earnings inequality, but this was offset by changes in returns to schooling. Inequality in completed years of education has declined since apartheid while earnings inequality has not fallen.
papers.contribution: Analyzes theoretically and empirically how earnings inequality responds to returns to schooling that rise at some levels and fall at others, over 1994-2019.
papers.ident: Decomposition of earnings inequality into education distribution and returns to schooling effects.
papers.dataDetail: South African household and labour data, 1994-2019.

papers.title: Settlement of Litigation May Increase or Decrease Deterrence and Social Welfare
papers.summary: Settlement raises plaintiffs' expected return and therefore the probability of suit, which augments deterrence, but it lowers defendants' expected litigation costs, which dilutes deterrence. Suit requires that plaintiffs be willing to go to trial and that anticipated settlements exceed their pretrial costs.
papers.q: Does settlement of litigation raise or lower deterrence and social welfare?
papers.contribution: Identifies the net effect of settlement on deterrence and welfare in a model of accidents, liability and litigation.
papers.ident: Theory: model of accidents, liability and litigation with settlement.

papers.title: Shopping From Home
papers.q: How does working from home change shopping behavior and prices paid?
papers.summary: WFH increased online shopping and weekday store trips, and raised total spending through more quantity and range. It also raised prices paid and lowered price elasticities, concentrated among married households, especially when the new remote worker is male, with more trips but fewer minutes of shopping.
papers.contribution: Conducts a new survey on the Nielsen Consumer panel to study the impact of working from home on shopping.
papers.dataDetail: New survey on the Nielsen Consumer panel.

papers.title: Temperature and Arrests in Prohibition-era South Carolina
papers.summary: All-offense arrests are 21% lower at 35 degrees than at 70 degrees Fahrenheit, and arrests do not rise above 70. The same pattern of fewer arrests in the cold appears for violent, public order and low-level fraud arrests, and for men, Whites and Blacks.
papers.ident: Random within-month daily variation in temperature and precipitation.
papers.q: How did temperature affect arrests in Prohibition-era South Carolina?
papers.contribution: Estimates how random within-month daily temperature and precipitation affect arrests, using arrest records of a Prohibition-era southern city without air conditioning, with negative binomial regressions.
papers.dataDetail: Arrest records from a Prohibition-era South Carolina city and daily weather.

papers.title: Shielding Women from Violence: The Effects of Violence Prevention and Monitoring Centers on Intimate Partner Violence in Türkiye
papers.q: Do Violence Prevention and Monitoring Centers reduce intimate partner violence against women in Turkey?
papers.summary: Opening a center reduces female homicides, particularly by intimate partners, by approximately 20 percent, and reduces women's self-reported physical IPV by 20 percent, more so among younger and less-educated women. Centers mainly act by lowering barriers to help-seeking and improving coordination.
papers.ident: Staggered rollout of centers across Turkish provinces.
papers.contribution: Exploits the staggered rollout of centers across provinces, with complementary survey evidence.
papers.dataDetail: Province-level female homicide data and survey evidence on IPV exposure.

papers.title: Good Neighborhoods, Good Neighbors, Good Jobs?

authors.inst: The University of Texas at Austin
VIVE - The Danish Center for Social Science Research

papers.q: Do good neighborhoods improve adults' labor market outcomes and reduce crime?
papers.contribution: Examines high-needs families in Denmark quasi-randomly assigned to social housing in different neighborhoods.
papers.summary: A one standard deviation improvement in nearby neighborhood quality improves labor market outcomes by 0.08 standard deviations and reduces the likelihood of criminal conviction by 2.8 percent. The labor market effects are most consistent with job referrals from neighbors rather than local job availability.
papers.ident: Quasi-random assignment of families to social housing in different neighborhoods.
papers.dataDetail: Danish administrative data on social housing assignment, labor market outcomes and convictions.

papers.title: Household Responses to Personalized Risk Information
papers.q: How do households respond to personalized information about indoor air pollution?
papers.summary: Indoor PM2.5 declines by 2.5 micrograms per cubic meter over 12 weeks after installation, conditional on outdoor pollution, with larger effects for households with high initial pollution. The indoor-outdoor gradient declines over time, and households respond primarily through durable changes.
papers.contribution: Uses data from residential air quality monitors, exploiting installation timing and high-frequency PM2.5 readings, with machine learning to infer cooking and air purifier adoption.
papers.ident: Timing of monitor installation with high-frequency indoor and outdoor PM2.5 readings.
papers.dataDetail: Residential air quality monitor readings of fine particulate matter.

papers.title: Job Loss and Health Insurance Coverage Before and After the Affordable Care Act
papers.q: How did the Affordable Care Act change the insurance consequences of job loss?
papers.summary: Before 2014, job loss reduced coverage by approximately 16 percentage points for over a year. After the ACA, declines are about 10 percentage points with faster recovery, reflecting higher baseline public coverage and smaller post-displacement losses, mostly for middle income workers.
papers.ident: Matched event study of displaced workers, before and after the ACA.
papers.contribution: Uses matched event-study models on longitudinal survey data to estimate the effects of displacement on coverage before and after the ACA's main provisions.
papers.dataDetail: Longitudinal survey data on displaced workers and insurance coverage.

papers.title: Expanding Paternity Leave: Effects on Beliefs, Norms, and Gender Gaps

authors.inst: Center for Economic and Policy Research
Center for Economic and Policy Research

papers.q: Can expanding earmarked paternity leave shift gender norms and narrow gender gaps?
papers.summary: The reform substantially reallocated leave from mothers to fathers, made parents more supportive of paternity leave, shifted gender-role beliefs in a progressive direction and reduced perceived differences in childcare ability. The earnings gap falls by 34pp in the first year after childbirth and by 2.8pp in the second.
papers.ident: Regression discontinuity around the Danish paternity leave reform.
papers.contribution: Exploits a major expansion of earmarked paternity leave in Denmark with a regression discontinuity design, combining new survey data with administrative records.
papers.conclusion: Policy can meaningfully influence beliefs, norms and gender inequality.
papers.dataDetail: New survey data linked to Danish administrative records.

papers.title: Great Expectations: Responses to Current and Future Transfers for Low-Income Individuals
papers.q: How does the expectation of aid change behavior among low-income individuals?
papers.summary: Both recipients and those promised cash increase their labor supply and investment, while immediate transfers also raise household expenditures and savings. The results are inconsistent with standard life-cycle models and better explained by a model where the transfer raises individual labor productivity.
papers.ident: Four-arm randomized trial comparing immediate cash with promised future cash.
papers.contribution: Separates expectations effects from direct resource effects by comparing the promise of a program to the program itself, in a four-arm randomized trial of cash transfers in Uganda.
papers.dataDetail: Four-arm randomized controlled trial of cash transfers in Uganda.

papers.title: Valuation of Regulatory Risk on Pharmaceutical R&D
papers.q: How do regulatory shocks change the value of pharmaceutical R&D?
papers.summary: Calibrated to an incremental CNS program, project value at initiation is highly right-skewed, with a mean of USD 69.6m but a negative median. Regulatory risk mainly compresses the upside, and both shorter effective exclusivity and price controls substantially weaken investment incentives even at moderate probability.
papers.ident: Quantitative: calibrated real options model of drug development.
papers.contribution: Develops a real options valuation model of drug R&D with sequential clinical investment, technical failure, stochastic costs, uncertain cash flows and optimal abandonment, including exclusivity and price-control shocks.
papers.dataDetail: Calibration to an incremental CNS drug program.

papers.title: The Local Origins of Business Formation: Entry as a Two-Stage Process
papers.contribution: Uses linked administrative microdata on the universe of US business applications and their transition into employer firms to model entry in two stages.
papers.summary: The application and transition margins are distinct and associate differently with local conditions. High-startup locations have high application intensity, while low-startup locations have low transition rates.
papers.q: Is business entry a two-stage process of application and transition to employer firm?
papers.dataDetail: Linked administrative data on all US business applications and employer firm transitions.

papers.title: Government Funding and the Direction of Academic Energy Research
papers.q: Does targeted government funding change the direction of academic clean energy research?
papers.contribution: Combines text and regression analyses of Department of Energy and National Science Foundation grants to compare publication trajectories of funded scientists with matched comparisons.
papers.summary: The paper asks whether scientists change their research focus in response to targeted funding opportunities such as ARPA-E, and what kinds of calls best attract new researchers. Little causal evidence exists linking funding to research direction outside health sciences.
papers.ident: Publication trajectories of funded scientists compared with matched non-funded scientists.
papers.dataDetail: Department of Energy and National Science Foundation grants and associated publications.

papers.title: Public Finance in the Age of AI: A Primer
papers.q: How should taxation adapt if transformative AI erodes labor income and human consumption as tax bases?
papers.contribution: Examines optimal taxation across two stages of AI-driven transformation, treating the taxation of autonomous AGI systems as an optimal harvesting problem.
papers.summary: If AI displaces human labor, consumption taxation may become the primary revenue instrument and differential commodity taxation regains relevance. If autonomous AGI systems produce most economic value, taxing human consumption may become inadequate.
papers.ident: Theory: optimal taxation in two stages of AI transformation.

papers.title: Bank Runs and Interest Rates: A Revolving Lines Perspective
papers.q: How do interest rates affect the risk of runs on revolving credit lines?
papers.summary: Corporate revolving lines are demandable claims, so widespread drawdowns can destabilize banks, but utilization is sensitive to interest rates. A run on credit lines is less likely when interest rates are high and can introduce vulnerabilities when policy rates are lowered.
papers.ident: Interest rate discontinuity embedded in commercial credit contracts.
papers.contribution: Uses an interest rate discontinuity embedded in commercial credit contracts to propose a methodology for estimating the elasticity of credit demand and measuring precautionary drawdowns.
papers.dataDetail: Commercial credit line contracts and drawdowns.

papers.title: Trading Goods for Lives: NAFTA’s Mortality Impacts and Implications
papers.q: How did exposure to NAFTA affect local mortality in the United States?
papers.summary: More exposed areas experienced sustained increases in mortality over 15 years, for all broad demographic groups and especially working-age men. Declines in manufacturing employment raise local mortality, while declines in non-manufacturing employment reduce it.
papers.contribution: Estimates mortality effects of local labor market exposure to NAFTA and compares them with other local labor market contractions.
papers.ident: Local labor market exposure to NAFTA tariff reductions.

papers.title: The Promise of Microbial Fertilizer for Affordable and Sustainable Food Production in Africa
papers.summary: Yields increase significantly, by up to 110% for some farmers, with lower environmental impact than synthetic products. This suggests biofertilizers could improve food security and child nutrition in Africa.

papers.summary: The interaction with other risks transforms the risk protection health insurance provides. Standard contracts amplify other risks by subsidizing normal goods and undoing protection from discounts, charity care and bad debt, while contracts limiting out-of-pocket spending relative to income could give better protection.
papers.q: How does health insurance change consumption risk when other risks are present?
papers.contribution: Uses several approaches to study how health insurance interacts with income risk and other risks for US households.

papers.title: Foreign Currency as a Barrier to International Trade: Evidence from Brazil
papers.q: Does dependence on foreign currency act as a barrier to trade?
papers.summary: Local currency adoption significantly increased export values, with effects concentrated among non-commodity exporters.
papers.ident: Triple difference across municipalities with varying bank access and across destinations around the 2008 payments system.
papers.contribution: Exploits the 2008 introduction of a bilateral payments system between Brazil and Argentina that eliminated the US dollar as vehicle currency, with a triple-difference design.
papers.conclusion: Foreign currency dependence is a meaningful barrier to emerging market trade.
papers.dataDetail: Firm-level exports from Brazilian municipalities.

papers.title: Human capital, unequal opportunities and productivity convergence: A global historical perspective, 1800–2100
papers.q: How did human capital and unequal opportunities shape productivity convergence from 1800 to 2100?
papers.summary: The title indicates a global historical study of human capital, unequal opportunities and productivity convergence from 1800 to 2100.

papers.title: Central bank reputation with noise
papers.q: How does noise affect central bank reputation?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of central bank reputation with noise.

papers.title: Firm and labor adjustments to FDI liberalization
papers.q: How does liberalizing outward FDI affect manufacturers and their domestic workers?
papers.summary: Targeted manufacturers were on average 10% more likely to invest in China. Their domestic incumbent workers were more likely to change jobs, stayed employed fewer years and had lower wages in subsequent years.
papers.ident: Matched difference-in-differences comparing manufacturers targeted by the 2001 policy with non-targeted ones.
papers.contribution: Uses a matched difference-in-differences strategy around Taiwan's 2001 liberalization allowing 122 electronic products to be produced in China.
papers.dataDetail: Taiwanese electronic manufacturers and matched worker data.

papers.title: Fiscal capacity and capital misallocation: the economic costs of tax evasion
papers.q: How does tax evasion affect fiscal capacity and capital misallocation?
papers.summary: The title indicates a study of fiscal capacity, capital misallocation and the economic costs of tax evasion.

papers.title: Intersectoral demand linkages: Good shocks, bad outcomes?
papers.q: When are sector-specific price shocks magnified or dampened in general equilibrium?
papers.summary: Cobb-Douglas or CES preferences with monopolistic competition always yield welfare gains from a positive shock, but a positive sectoral shock may cause aggregate losses with departures from either. Shocks propagate via consumer preferences here, unlike production networks in Baqaee and Farhi.
papers.ident: Sufficient statistics: welfare multiplier for sectoral shocks under homothetic preferences.
papers.contribution: Develops a framework with homothetic sectoral preferences and derives a welfare multiplier, a sufficient statistic for the share of a shock's direct effect that materializes in the aggregate.

papers.title: Well-being Increases in Age Among Workers: Evidence From 103 Countries
papers.q: Does workers' well-being rise with age across the world?
papers.summary: In 103 countries (60%) workers' well-being rises with age and ill-being falls with age, a relationship that has strengthened over time in some countries. Non-workers' patterns differ and are sensitive to survey mode, with a U-shape in web interviews that is less clear in telephone interviews.
papers.contribution: Examines how workers' and non-workers' well-being varies by age across 171 countries in eight international surveys.
papers.dataDetail: Eight international surveys covering 171 countries.

papers.title: Wedges: A Microeconomic Perspective on Misallocation
papers.contribution: Takes stock of the micro-development literature on wedges and presents a general framework distinguishing technological wedges from distortionary wedges.
papers.summary: Technological wedges are present even in the social planner's efficient allocation, whereas distortionary wedges arise only in market equilibrium, so not all wedges are distortionary. The chapter argues interactions among wedges are pervasive and reviews empirical findings on taxes, regulations and political connections.
papers.q: What have we learned about wedges as indicators of misallocation?

papers.title: Estimating Demand Systems with Bidding Data
papers.summary: Using Canadian Treasury bill auction data, dealer demand is elastic and bills of different maturities act as weak substitutes. Recovering demand lets policymakers isolate cross-asset spillovers from strategic bid shading.
papers.q: How can demand systems across multiple assets be estimated from bidding data without price instruments?
papers.contribution: Introduces a framework using price-quantity limit orders, allowing flexible substitution patterns, with identification for price-taking and strategic investors.
papers.ident: Structural: demand estimation from bidding data without price instruments.
papers.dataDetail: Canadian Treasury bill auction bids.

papers.title: Poverty and Dependency in the United States, 1939–2023
papers.contribution: Creates a post-tax post-transfer income measure for the 1940, 1950 and 1960 Censuses through imputations of taxes, transfers and perquisites, consistent with full income measures for later years.
papers.summary: From 1939 to 1963 poverty fell by 29 percentage points, with larger declines for Black people and children. Absolute poverty continued to fall after the War on Poverty's declaration but the pace was no faster.
papers.q: How did absolute poverty in the US change before and after the War on Poverty?
papers.ident: Descriptive: full-income poverty measures across 1939-2023.
papers.dataDetail: Decennial Censuses 1940-1960 with imputed taxes and transfers, linked to later full income measures.

papers.title: Is the Environmental Exposure Gap Shrinking? Evidence from an Extreme Multi-exposure Index
papers.q: Is the gap in exposure to extreme multiple environmental stressors shrinking?
